This study investigates the relationship between the ground state of the Schrödinger operator, $H = -\Delta + V$, and a particular mathematical space known as the spectral Barron space. We examine specific conditions under which the ground state, denoted $\phi_0$, resides within a Barron space characterized by the constants $C_1$ and $C_2$. The results provide precise estimates for the Barron radius and norm when the conditions are met. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of our findings for the universal approximation capabilities of two-neural network models. Notably, we demonstrate that if the Barron radius is finite, at least one neural network component can be pre-trained and remain unchanged, while achieving an approximation error of order $d^{-1/2}$ with high probability for data drawn from a probability density function with finite Barron norm.

The intricately connected brain network is a subject of significant research, yet its understanding of brain activity remains limited.  For modelling purposes, researchers are increasingly turning to model organisms with complex behaviours.  Given the close evolutionary ties between humans and C. elegans, this small organism's response to various stimuli and structural features make it an ideal model for simulating brain activity.  With the aid of modern computational tools and techniques, it's now feasible to simulate C. elegans' behaviour more accurately.  However, accurately simulating the small organism's movement requires precise models of its anatomy and dynamics.  Despite existing models of the nervous system guiding the simulation, a model of the physical body is still lacking.  Our study presents a comprehensive physics-based model of the C. elegans body that realistically accounts for the effects of food and environmental factors.  Using machine learning algorithms, the model successfully replicates the movement of real organisms and exhibits robustness in its results.  Our model's ability to accurately simulate C. elegans movement using only basic physical laws and data highlights its promise as a simulation tool.  This approach could serve as a starting point for further simulation of the small organism.

A new class of random permutations is introduced, characterized by defining a longest path from the root to a leaf within associated rooted tree structures. These permutations and their corresponding trees exhibit a specific large-scale behavior, converging to the Young measure in distribution. Notably, the length of the longest path converges to the Geometric distribution in dimensions of 2 or greater. Associated random trees also demonstrate a specific, two-dimensional, scale-invariant limit in the appropriately rescaled format.

A strong Gelfand pair (G,H) is defined by a group G and subgroup H, 
with every irreducible character of H resulting in a multiplicity-free 
character of G. Specifically, we identify the strong Gelfand pairs of SL(2, 
p) when p is a prime number.

The study of electromagnetic form factors of the $P=S\bar{Q}q$ pentaquark states
offers valuable insights into their internal structure. Using the $qq'\bar{Q}\bar{S}$
cluster model, researchers have made predictions about the electromagnetic radii of
these pentaquarks, which are characterized by the properties of their constituent
clusters. In this study, they investigate the electromagnetic form factors of the
isoscalar $J^P=0^+$ pentaquark states, which are composed of the lightest strange
quark $S=\pm 1$ and have baryon number $B=0$. Using the $d\bar{Q}$ and $Sq$ cluster
assignment, they calculate the electromagnetic radii of these pentaquarks, which are
found to be significantly different from those of the $Q\bar{Q}s d$ pentaquarks.
Moreover, they have discovered that the $P=S=\bar{Q}q$ pentaquark states, which are
composed of the up, down, and charm or bottom light quarks, have unique
electromagnetic properties, which are dependent on the quark flavor.
This paper proves that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a given field possesses a specific characteristic - nilpotency, building on a previous discovery that these algebras are solvable.

This research examines the scattering theory for a causal cubic Schrödinger equation with a reciprocal quadratic potential, which models the interaction between a background potential field and a quantum field. By leveraging the weighted energy space and equation decomposition, the study establishes space-time estimates for the defined system. It is then demonstrated that in a non-interacting scenario, the estimated norms are conserved. Furthermore, the results show that both the interacting and non-interacting fields exhibit conserved properties. Ultimately, the study proves that all existing initial data result in scattering solutions, with the analysis extended to a more complex potential scenario.

Consider an N-station network where K_N customers reside, each station functioning as a queuing system with M_N single-server stations operating under a first-come, first-served basis. Each station is characterized by an infectious rate λ_N, a removal rate μ_N, and a service rate γ_N. Customers' behavior is such that if a customer is not currently serving, there is a probability θ_N that the customer departs the current station and moves to a randomly chosen one. The paper derives the necessary and sufficient conditions for the long-term behavior of the stochastic process describing the number of customers at each station. Specifically, it focuses on the scenario where the probability θ_N of transitioning between stations converges to a value θ as N approaches infinity. The analysis shows that the stochastic process converges in a appropriate manner to a birth-death process if and only if the inequality λ_N < μ_N holds, with λ_N and γ_N also converging to λ and γ. The paper provides an explicit expression for the stationary distribution of the birth-death process.

Numerical studies of the K2-138 planetary system have been conducted to assess the stability of various orbital configurations. Initial analyses of 100 million years of nearly stable and stable configurations involving only three planets revealed a 1:2 resonance between planet c and f, accompanied by 3:2 resonances between planet c and d, and confirmed previous findings regarding the likelihood of this orbital arrangement in 80% of these simulations. Furthermore, 1 million-year simulations of stable configurations involving all five planets also supported these results. Subsequently, 100 million-year simulations of configurations with only planet f, g, and h revealed the presence of 1:2 resonations between these planets in 70% of stable cases. Conversely, 1 million-year simulations of stable configurations involving all seven planets have been performed and have shown the presence of 3:2 resonations among planets g, e, and d, as well as 1:2 resonations among planets e and d, f and g, and g and e.

We establish connections between the Gelfand--Graev modules for central covers, the Euler--Poincar\'e polynomial of the Arnold--Brieskorn manifold, and the quantum affine Schur--Weyl duality via a permutation representation of the Weyl group, which governs these three objects.

The SiD Detector is one of the two validated detector designs for the future ILC, specifically tailored to meet precision requirements for the physics it aims to explore. Central to the SiD's design philosophy is the achievement of highly precise momentum measurements, facilitated by its advanced tracking system which combines two high-resolution silicon vertex and tracking detectors with powerful trigger chambers. Alongside the precision measurement capability, the SiD also prioritizes high particle identification accuracy through its extensive calorimeter system, complemented by its forward region covering the beam pipe, and features robust hadron and lepton shielding to ensure optimal performance.

The structure of water ice is highly complex, with numerous crystalline forms. Using a novel metric, we can differentiate between theoretical models of liquid water and various types of ice (hexagonal, cubic, tetrahedral, and amorphous). This metric, based on a graph representation of molecular connectivity, enables the differentiation of ice types with a threshold value. Additionally, our methodology successfully distinguishes between hexagonal and cubic ice detected in an ion trap experiment. This graph representation can be applied to other systems to identify structural characteristics.

A set of experiments utilizing STM and AFM on High-quality HOPG and Si surfaces were conducted using a home-built UHV-STM/AFM system equipped with a Si wafer as an AFM reference. The measured lattice constants for HOPG and Si, when compared to the literature values, showed discrepancies of 0.0001 nm (or 0.07%) and 0.0009 nm (or 0.09%) respectively, indicating a high level of accuracy. The experimental setup and procedures are detailed to provide a comprehensive reference for other researchers, and the results demonstrate the precision and effectiveness of the system in measuring atomic-scale lattice constants.

The Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs has amassed substantial material over the years, encompassing nearly 800 theorems and lemmas that have been proven using various methods.  As the repository continues to grow, its vastness poses a challenge in accessing and understanding its contents.  To address this issue, we propose a novel approach centered around connecting formal proofs with external resources, thereby making it easier to navigate the archive.  Furthermore, we introduce a formal method for representing graph structures and a corresponding tool for analyzing network architectures, thereby further enhancing the accessibility of the archive's contents.

In situ data from the heliosphere is often characterized by complex oscillations, allowing researchers to apply a versatile technique known as audification to enhance comprehension. By converting these oscillations into sound, researchers can identify patterns and structures that may not be apparent in visual representations. Based on prior successful applications, audification techniques have recently been used to explore relationships between various space plasma components, yielding unexpected acoustic correlations. Furthermore, researchers have applied an audio processing technique known as spectrogram clustering to identify and categorize distinct, recurring sounds produced by space plasma. By analyzing acoustic spectra, researchers can identify these clusters, which correspond to specific plasma states, thereby providing a potential method for detecting spatial and temporal plasma transitions within the heliosphere.

A new family of rotating black brane solutions in four-dimensional spacetime, including a non-zero mass charge, is developed with non-trivial electromagnetic and scalar (dilaton) field configurations. The black brane has both non-zero angular momentum and non-zero electric field. The solution is time-independent and possesses electric field lines perpendicular to the horizons. A phase transition diagram is created based on the behavior of specific charges and electric field. When the coupling constant between the dilaton and electromagnetic fields is less than approximately 0.62, the extremal rotating black brane exhibits thermal stability. Conversely, when the coupling constant exceeds this value, the same black brane exhibits thermal instability.

The search for effective text representations is an ongoing priority in the field of NLP.
While BERT has set a new standard for text representation, its design is primarily
driven by performance in NLP tasks. In this paper, we suggest that text
representation should be understood through the lens of human memory. Following
this idea, we introduce MEMO, a novel text representation model inspired by how
humans recall events. MEMO encines text as a sequence of facts and stores these
facts in a knowledge graph format, allowing for flexible retrieval. To enhance
memory storage, we employ a dynamic memory network, and improve memory recall
through the application of reinforcement learning. Various experiments indicate
that MEMO surpasses existing methods in cross-cultural name relation detection,
cross-lingual knowledge enhancement, and visual question answering.

For any real number q, such that its absolute value is less than one, we look at the universal C*-algebra generated by q-canonical commutation relations in the context of a countable, infinitely large set. It is known that when we assign a specific type of structure to this algebra through a isomorphism with a product of q-canonical relations in each individual set, multiple distinct Fock representations result. These distinct representations are known to be radically different in the sense that they cannot be obtained from each other in a way that preserves their structure. In this investigation, we analyze specific endomorphisms of the countable set mentioned earlier and investigate how these map to distinct Fock representations, revealing that there is a precise relationship between them. In the case of finite q, this analysis further shows that each countable set with an infinite number of elements maps to a unique Fock representation in a way that preserves structure.

A small-step operational semantics for a language is defined as a transition system where a configuration can only move to another configuration of the same type. A common scenario arises when the definition of a function includes recursive calls to that same function, and a naive small-step semantics can lead to a contradiction by requiring a configuration to transition to a configuration of the same type, but already transitioned from a different configuration. To resolve this issue, we propose a modification of the small-step semantics that utilizes a "stalled" configuration to prevent the contradiction, and we have proven the correctness and utility of this modified semantics through its equivalence with both the unmodified small-step semantics and the large-step operational semantics.

We've developed new theoretical models to explain the young stellar object TW Hydrae's complex emission pattern. Our models consider the effects of photoevaporation, accounting for molecular hydrogen, the main star, and other spectral lines. Photoevaporation is found to be a crucial factor in explaining a broad mid-infrared emission feature, including its response to stellar outbursts. When combined with data from the OI $1304$ line, a standard photoevaporation model accurately explains all observed fluxes. Additionally, our findings indicate that a carbon monoxide molecule, the $S$ $(1-0)$ line could potentially explain an unexplained short-period variability.

We prove factorizations for Chebyshev polynomials of the third and fourth kinds, determining the unique ways to express $\pm P_3^k(x)$ and $\pm P_4^k(x)$ as a product of distinct Chebyshev polynomials $P_{q_1}(x) P_{q_2}(x) \cdots P_{q_m}(x)$, with $m \geq 2$ and $3 \leq q_1 \leq q_2 \leq \cdots \leq q_m$. The expected explicit factorizations for $P_3^k$ and $P_4^k$ are found, along with the highest possible value of $m$ in these factorizations.

This research assesses the effectiveness of a Fuzzy Inference System in differentiating between internal faults and transient disturbances affecting ISPAR transformers. The classifier exhibits a remarkable 99.5% accuracy in distinguishing transient signals, while also achieving 99.9% accuracy in correctly categorizing internal faults. The implemented classifier can distinguish transient signals such as fluctuating loads, harmonics, transient impacts, and transient faults, in addition to internal failures including core displacement, tilt with stator contact, and rotor with stator contact. The internal faults and transient signals used in this study were generated using PSCAD.

The performance of a multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) system is influenced by several factors such as imperfect channel state information, limited knowledge of these factors, and constraints on this mappable information. This work investigates the relationship between these constraints and spectral efficiency losses. A unified framework is proposed to quantify this loss due to the inconsistency of mappable and actual channels. This framework is applied to multicast beamforming scenarios where the same data stream is sent to multiple users, and this beamforming may or may not be adapted to each user's channel. The general approach involves introducing auxiliary variables to measure spectral efficiency losses and initially focuses on designing beamforming vectors that maximize a lower bound for these losses under various constraints. The results show that the designed beamforming performs comparably to the optimal one when channel state information is perfect, and this holds true for both adapted and non-adapted users. Theoretical analysis also reveals that this performance equivalence holds asymptotically with an increasing number of users.

A function from natural numbers to natural numbers is considered near-exponential if it's confined between two shifted and scaled exponential functions with slightly varying bases. This type of function can be uniquely defined by its restriction under a shifted range, meaning for any function with this characteristic, there exists a corresponding, distinct function where the values of the original match the characteristics of the original after shifting the input. This principle of uniqueness is proven and has a counterpart in terms of limits - the pointwise limit of any sequence of near-exponential functions is either a constant function or remains near-exponential. This theorem is the foundational element for proving the total computability of the inductive Hat problem.

We demonstrate exponential stability of a stretched Euler-Bernoulli beam on a star-shaped graph with three edges and boundaries connecting to a rigid hoop. By introducing a localized damping and delay feedback control on one of the beams, we achieve asymptotic stability of the system. Notably, under this stability, the eigenvectors of the associated operator exhibit a specific property: they have zero components on the two undamped edges. Furthermore, using the Lagrange method, we show the set of eigenvectors corresponding to eigenvalues of the stationary system forms a Riesz basis for $L^2$ on the graph.

A new machine learning model based on Bayesian principles and the energy of nuclear masses was developed for predicting nuclear masses. It uses an expanded version of the 57 most important observables from a previous study, which includes single-particle energies, and achieves a 99.9% accuracy with an average error margin of less than 10 keV for test sets consisting of 10,000 masses from the FRDM, 1000 masses from the SHEN, and 1000 masses from the SHEN's test set. Its code is available online at https://github.com/DeepNuclear/frdm_ml.

Superconducting quantum circuits are becoming more sensitive to dielectric loss, which poses challenges for understanding superconducting materials at cryogenic temperatures. An innovative technique, employing lock-in detection and a superconducting resonator, has been developed to precisely measure dielectric loss tangent. Using this approach, the cryogenic loss tangent of silicon substrates and strontium titanate coatings was studied. By modulating the processing parameters of silicon wafers and varying their orientation, we found that certain wafers exhibit significantly lower dielectric loss than others, which could lead to better circuit performance. Furthermore, by coating these same wafers with strontium titanate and repeating the process, we discovered that this material could reduce dielectric loss by over an order of magnitude, which could improve the sensitivity of superconducting quantum circuits.

A moving dielectric medium can alter the Fresnel-Fizeau optical drag effect on propagating light. In the context of **gauge theories**, optical effects arise naturally from photons interacting with a medium. When the medium is in motion, a photon can be viewed as a **dressed photon**, which differs significantly in its properties. A photon-drag model in a uniform flow of the medium is studied, and it's shown that this process results in the emission of a damped, redshifted photon. This optical drag effect is equivalent to the emission of a **dressed photon**, which behaves differently depending on the velocity of the medium. A comparison with existing experimental data on photon drag is conducted.

This paper introduces an exact algorithm to efficiently compute the most adverse scenario for two-stage robust optimization problems with binary integer first-stage variables and continuous recourse variables, particularly in the context of robust network design problems. Given the computational limitations of existing algorithms for related network design problems, this algorithm relies on solving a mixed-integer linear program rather than a mixed-integer nonlinear program. A dual formulation is derived to ease the computation of worst-case scenarios and accompanying dual subgradients for the corresponding dual problem. A cutting-plane algorithm incorporating these subgradients is proposed to solve the dual problem, demonstrating the method on robust network design problems and showing its reduced dependence on the size of the network and the size of the flow units.

The understanding of urban behavior is heavily reliant on the analysis of movement patterns, which is crucial for developing transportation systems, mapping traffic congestion, and creating emergency evacuation plans. Traditionally, this involved analyzing data from various sensors, but recent advancements allow accessing detailed real estate transaction data through multiple online sources. By combining such data, researchers can infer people's movement habits, filling gaps in the analysis and offering new insights. Notably, property transaction records provide concrete evidence of individuals' long-term relocations, making them a valuable resource to study. By examining the time intervals between these relocations, researchers can identify different migration patterns, ultimately revealing the underlying factors driving individuals' movement. This novel approach is demonstrated through the analysis of the Barcelona city dataset, showcasing its potential application.

The advent of vast datasets has led to an explosion in patterns being discovered, yet their abundance makes it increasingly difficult to grasp the overall distribution of patterns. To address this challenge, we've developed a novel framework for understanding patterns in large datasets using vast arrays of data. Our framework employs a combination of clustering, dimensionality reduction, visualization, and statistical analysis to facilitate a deeper comprehension of patterns. We've put our framework to the test using a comprehensive dataset of all possible word bigrams from the entire corpus of the Wikipedia project, thereby showcasing its efficacy.

Deep learning models, including Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), typically require substantial computational resources for training. Transfer learning presents an alternative approach by enabling models to utilize pre-existing knowledge gained from training on related tasks. Our research focuses on transfer learning for GNNs, a relatively under-researched area. We have developed the first benchmark for transfer learning in GNNs, consisting of three distinct tasks, and conducted an in-depth evaluation of various transfer learning methods. Notably, direct parameter fine-tuning achieved state-of-the-art performance, outperforming more complex methods that attempt to decouple weight transfers.

A collaborative filtering system predicts user preferences by identifying patterns between users with similar tastes, where their preferences are inversely proportional to their distance in a feature space. To address the challenge of feature selection, we explore the benefits of using automatically generated semantic concepts to create a contextual framework for analysis. We propose an algorithm that identifies the optimal set of features from item metadata by measuring the separation of latent user preferences within this framework. We demonstrate our approach through experiments on the MovieLens dataset, showing that optimizing the feature set enhances the performance of the recommendation system.

We establish a memory- and time-efficient approach for identifying top-heavy-hitters in data streams. Our method achieves O(θ⁻²ρ⁻²log log n) word storage and processing a total of O(θ⁻²ρ⁻²log n) elements, where 0 < θ < 1 is the heavy-hitter fraction and 0 < ρ < 1 is the failure tolerance. Here, the algorithm detects the top k*×θ data items with at most ρ* error for k* being the top storage needs. Our approach improves on the current storage and time requirements for the case where θ is the storage needs. Our approach improves on the current storage requirements for the case where θ is the storage needs. Our approach improves on the current storage requirements for the case where θ is the storage needs. For instance, to guarantee an error rate of at most 0.2 for the top 10% data items in a stream of n items, the current storage requirements are O(n) while our approach is O(sqrt(log n))

We investigated the long-term behavior of two key observables - static magnetic susceptibility and dynamic susceptibility - for Heisenberg magnets by employing Edakura's time-dependent variational Monte Carlo method. Through our research, we discovered that as the momentum vector approaches zero, a significant deviation occurs in the momentum-based dependence of the static susceptibility. This phenomenon is attributed to the correlation length. Furthermore, we found that in low-temperature regimes or when the correlation length is substantial,a significant deviation occurs in the momentum-based dependence of the dynamic susceptibility. Notably, we found that the dynamic susceptibility deviates from the standard Moriya formula.

A monolithically integrated multi-grating system has been proposed and implemented to create an optical dipole trap for holding individual Rubidium atoms with a repulsive potential. Using 3D simulations, a significant reduction in the numerical model's complexity is possible by incorporating only the relevant parts of the device's geometry into finite element simulations. Moreover, using a reduced geometry model enables the circuit's compactness and power consumption characteristics to be studied at a much lower resolution 3D model scale. Experimental results obtained using Rubidium atoms demonstrate the effectiveness of the on-chip multi-grating system in producing a ~100 μm diameter optical dipole trap capable of trapping and holding individual Rubidium atoms.

Building on Sodemann and Fu's theory of the nonlinear Hall effect established in 2015, 
this study expands their framework to encompass Bloch electrons that incorporate both spin-orbit coupling and magnetic order. 
Key findings include the derivation of a set of Berry curvature dipole tensor elements from momentum-space nonlinear Hall currents. 
These effective tensor elements are influenced by momentum skewing induced by both spin polarization and the presence of odd parity odd Fermi surface displacements of the Bloch electrons. 
Notably, this research substantiates the coexistence of displacement currents and anomalous velocity currents within a unified framework, extending the scope of Sodemann and Fu's original work beyond its constraints.

In control and economics, control problems, characterized by continuous dynamics, cost assessments, and constraint specifications, constitute a fundamental class of tasks. When solutions cannot be derived analytically, numerical techniques such as time-discretization, time-discretization with mirror mapping, and NLP-solving are applied. These approaches, however, frequently result in suboptimal continuous solutions due to the optimal solutions of the corresponding discrete problems not converging to the true optimal solutions as the discretization becomes increasingly dense. Our work presents a theoretical framework for generating continuous solutions, based on the NLP solutions of a time-discretized version of the control problem, by minimizing an adjusted objective function involving additional penalty terms that reflect the cost of control and the residual suboptimality gap. We further propose a practical algorithm, by successively solving a time-discretization, evaluation, and gap-estimation steps and utilizing the estimations to guide the discretization process, and demonstrate through case studies that this algorithm can effectively tackle challenging control problems, by balancing global optimality and continuity in solutions.

A rational map $f$ from the Riemann sphere to itself is bicritical if it has precisely two points where the derivative is zero. We identify the groups that can be formed as groups of deck transformations of iterations of such bicritical maps, providing a complete classification up to isomorphism.

Two-dimensional semiconducting devices have significant potential in future
nanoelectronics, and transition-metal dichalceneides (TMDs) are promising
materials for this application. The key to the success of TMDs lies in their
excellent electron and hole mobility, excellent thermal conductivity, and
outstanding piezoelectricity. The unique properties of the individual monolayers
are essential to the success of the materials, and researchers have been
investigating the effects of different metal combinations. Theoretical studies
have shown that molybdenum and tungsten monolayers have excellent
electronic characteristics, but experimental studies have been limited. This
research presents the first comprehensive study of the surface properties of
molybdenum and tungsten monolayers using advanced molecular dynamics simulations.
The results show that both M-X monolayers have excellent heat transfer properties
and strong resistance to surface contamination, and that tungsten may perform
better in certain conditions. The findings suggest that both molybdenum and
tungsten monolayers have excellent potential for TMD-based nanoelectronics
applications.

A widely used mathematical framework, delta lenses, enables model-based software to effectively handle complex transformations between multiple models. However, traditional delta lenses lack adaptability to dynamic adjustments of their core principles, restricting software application developers to initially established optimization criteria when applying these lenses. To overcome this limitation, we have developed a comprehensive framework to optimize delta lenses through a two-pronged approach consisting of (a) a composability method for delta lenses and (b) an advanced delta lens editing technique. By utilizing our composability construction, model-based software application developers can establish learnable interfaces, thereby facilitating adaptable and composable optimization processes. Furthermore, we have demonstrated a specific lens editing approach based on fiber categories, which allows developers to establish optimal representations for optimization in model transformations. This contribution effectively bridges the gap between theoretical model transformations and practical software implementation, thereby addressing a long-standing challenge in the field of languages and software engineering.

This research focuses on developing estimates for oscillatory integrals with stationary phase points of any order, a more complex version of the classic Stokes phenomenon, by utilizing the wave packet decomposition from \cite{CDS}. Our findings surpass earlier estimates established by Sogge and Mei-Zworski in a few crucial aspects, and in scenarios of high complexity, they even yield sharp estimates. The approach is more versatile than a numerical simulation method proposed by Burq and Zelditch, applicable in various contexts such as the manifold setting of \cite{CDS}.

A new model of the Boltzmann equation is introduced, incorporating an adjustment term, $R_{\epsilon}$, to account for certain aspects when seeking steady-state solutions near the continuum state. However, it has been demonstrated that achieving a precise solution, where the residue is exactly equal to zero, is generally not possible due to the inherent $L^2$-orthogonality condition. Consequently, the problem of finding an exact solution is replaced with the task of minimizing the $L^2$-norm of the adjustment term, $R_{\epsilon}$. Numerical findings reveal that minimizing this term often results in the emergence of complex, non-physical phenomena.

The Hubble tension, with its varying degrees of multi-$\sigma$ discrepancies, has been observed, and our analysis reveals an analogous issue within the cosmic shear two-point correlation function. This particular data presentation is unique because it can be easily transformed into any other observable form. Furthermore, we discovered that when plotted against angular multipole $l$, the second-to-leading order term exhibits distinct peak characteristics. These additional peaks cannot be attributed to simple oscillations, suggesting instead, the possibility of a clustering origin. Additionally, the amplitude of the Hubble tension might be underestimated when considering this function.

Using proton-proton collision data with an integrated luminosity of 35.9 fb^-1, and acquired at a center-of-mass energy of 8 TeV with the CMS detector, this report presents a preliminary measurement of the Higgs-like boson's (H) mass in the H→ZZ*→llνν channel. The dataset encompasses Higgs boson production from multiple sources, such as gluon-gluon fusion, vector-boson fusion, and both photon and Z-boson fusion. Utilizing a constrained likelihood fit, the analysis determines the Higgs boson's mass in the H→ZZ→llνν channel. The results reveal an observed Higgs boson mass of 126.0±2.1 GeV, with a confidence level of 95%. Furthermore, this analysis yields insights into the Higgs boson's production cross-sections, suggesting that the latter may deviate from the Standard Model predictions.

We introduce a concept for the p-divisibility transposition of the Fourier coefficients 
of Siegel modular forms. This concept complements the Wilton result on p-divisibility for the Ramanujan $\tau$-function.

In 2002, Biss researched a type of fibration known as the rigid fibration (introduced in [Bi1]), exhibiting characteristics similar to those of covering spaces. A key discovery was made: a rigid fibration p over a topological space X with a simply connected domain corresponds to the covering space associated with X's universal infinite cyclic cover. Building on this concept, this paper introduces a generalized version - the covering fibration - extending the properties of rigid fibration. Covering fibration p over X with fibre F establishes an equivalence between p and the bundle of covering spaces over X's universal infinite cyclic cover constructed with F as the fibre in place. A local criterion for determining if p is a covering fibration is established. Furthermore, the paper explores the connections between covering fibration p and its corresponding homotopy fibration hf(p), as well as the relationships between the homotopy groups of p, hf(p), and the topological groupoid associated with p, which serves as a generalization of the deck transformation group when dealing with p as a rigid fibration. A specific example of a covering fibration is presented.

The phenomenon of the Pauli Exclusion Principle manifests itself when low-temperature 2D harmonic traps hold two ultra-cold $^6$Li atoms, resulting in the absence of Pauli blocking when they share the same quantum state, and a corresponding 100% activation when they occupy different states. The theory behind this phenomenon involves the precise mathematical description of interacting fermions in a potential well, which involves a complex equation that accurately models low-temperature behaviors. The theory further includes an algorithmic method for solving associated boundary equations over precise domains in the complex plane. The theory has been experimentally validated by a study published in 2018 by a research team at the Max Planck Institute, and further analysis revealed the existence of a specific complex curve related to light interactions.

A cutting-edge class of neural networks, called Zeroing Neural Networks (ZNNs), is increasingly being used to solve time-varying problems in real-time across various domains. The speed of ZNNs is heavily influenced by the rate at which their error decreases over time. In this study, we introduce the concept of the error decay floor (EDF) of a ZNN, along with its measurement techniques and calculation methods for both linear and nonlinear decay models. The paper then applies these measurements to compare the performance of two ZNN models, one using an exponential decay model and the other using a time-dependent decay model. The analysis demonstrates that adding a time-dependent term to the exponential decay model results in faster error reduction rates, thus outperforming the traditional exponential decay model.

Our vision system employs two complementary pathways to convey diverse visual data to the brain, with a proposed edge detection mechanism inspired by our color processing system. This proposed method leverages both types of pathways to achieve invariant edge detection under various lighting conditions. Our edge detection approach outperforms established methods on the PASCAL Visual Challenge 2012 dataset, particularly in challenging scenarios such as rain and fog.

The WHT pathloss function, a key element in wide-field X-ray telescope optimization, was developed by JWST. This pathloss function, defined over a spherical surface, assesses the image quality for every point on the sky relative to every axis orientation. As a result, the optimal mirror prescription for the WHT can be designed to create a uniform focal surface across the entire field of view. With an octopole component added to the WHT, researchers used octopolar optics and a spherical mirror to model the image quality and extend the telescope's field of regard. This led to the creation of a new pathloss function, S8, that incorporates the influence of the octopole component. Researchers found that the S8 function exhibits distinct features, specifically eight-fold symmetry and specific patterns of distortion, particularly at high off-axis angles. As a result, the WHT can achieve a more uniform image across the entire field of view when properly aligned.

The core of topological band theory, Bloch's theorem, is a fundamental concept in quantum materials research. Nevertheless, it is often difficult for students and experts to grasp the idea of Bloch states and their wavefunctions due to the complexity of their formal derivations. We have created and open-sourced user-friendly Python code to simplify and streamline the process of formulating Bloch states and their corresponding wavefunctions, making it more accessible to the research community.

Our proposed linguistic steganographic system is based on an LSTM neural network and aims to steganographically encode secret messages within steganographic stanzas of Georgian chazhura poems. We have developed and prototyped the system using the Keras deep learning framework, utilizing the existing corpus of Georgian chazhura poems. Preliminary results demonstrate the system's capability to accurately predict and generate steganographic stanzas, effectively concealing a target message. Moreover, our analysis of a related steganographic challenge employing an N-gram model supports the effectiveness and security of our LSTM-based approach.

Transmission system operators utilize unit commitment (UC) models to determine optimal system schedules for generation units. To streamline the solution process, operators often employ a constraint screening approach, which eliminates infeasible solutions beforehand by using simplified models based on load-flow models. Although these simplified models are effective in preventing nonsensical solutions, their models can become inaccurate with significant violations, rendering the screening process ineffective in such cases. To rectify this issue, this paper proposes replacing the traditional load-flow model with an explicit model grounded in graph neural networks. By leveraging this explicit model, researchers demonstrated that it can accurately predict key variables in test systems, thereby proving its utility in this context.

Measurements of magnetization were conducted under varying temperatures and hydrostatic pressures for $\eta$-Li$_2$IrO$_3$ across the temperature range from 2K to 30K with pressures up to 12GPa. As pressure was increased, we observed a notable decrease in the N\'eel temperature, $T_N$, at a rate of 0.3K/GPa, which was attributed to our findings. We also observed the emergence of an unusual low-temperature state below 4.5K with magnetic entropy values significantly higher than that expected for a ferromagnetic state with an effective magnetic moment of 1.08$\mu_B$. This phenomenon is attributed to the emergence of an exotic low-energy state as the system moves away from the ferromagnetic state due to an enhanced antiferromagnetic (AFM) exchange interaction. This resulting state is characterized by a high degree of quantum spin fluctuations. Our results demonstrate that this material can be manipulated through external pressure to access a variety of unconventional magnetic states.

A widely used technique in causal inference, synthetic control, creates a virtual group from parallel trends by combining panel data. However, existing synthetic control methods rely on specific models that assume certain patterns, which may not always hold. In an effort to address this issue, a new, more general method has been developed that is capable of utilizing panel data and makes fewer restrictive assumptions. This new method views the synthetic control problem as a problem of finding the best possible combination of panel data units that minimizes the difference between the treated and control groups. By using this more general method, researchers can apply it to both simple and more complex data sets. Simulation studies demonstrate the benefits of this new method when assumptions are violated, while applied work demonstrates its use in policy analysis.

Determining similarity between structured data sets, such as graphs, is an essential task in various applications. The Gromov-Wasserstein (GW) distance has emerged as a promising tool in this regard, effectively capturing the similarity between underlying graph structures. However, computing the GW distance is an intricate problem. Recent advancements in optimization techniques and deep learning have led to the development of more efficient algorithms. In this research, we introduce a novel approach to approximating the GW distance by leveraging tensor decomposition and an efficient optimization algorithm that leverages this structure. The proposed results demonstrate the convergence of our algorithm to a local minimum of the GW distance and validate this through experimental results.

A platinum foil with a mass of 100 grams was analyzed using a high-purity Germanium detector to detect double beta decays in its natural isotopes. The analysis, which was conducted over a 10-year period, has established limits on the half-life of double beta decays to various excited states of $^{^{194,196,198}Pt}$ with limits varying from $10^{20}$ to $10^{22}$ years. The degree of contamination that led to these findings is discussed.

Using a renormalization group-invariant mass renormalization scheme, we analyze the mass dependence of the renormalization constants of various operators crucial in QCD and QCD sum rules. These constants, however, cannot eliminate the renormalization scheme dependence entirely. Our analysis further demonstrates that an axial-anomaly equation exists, making the renormalization constants of pseudoscalar density and the mixed flavor components of the gluino-quark helicity currents invariant under renormalization, with implications for understanding QCD sum rules.

This research develops a novel, efficient, and straightforward approach to recovering high-quality images from both, two-color-dual-camera and single-monochrome-camera systems. We create a novel, dual-camera recovery technique that integrates color and single-channel images through a structured optimization process, resulting in enhanced noise removal and reduced degradation from color filters. In contrast to existing methods, our approach avoids costly computational procedures and color image image-to-image conversion. Additionally, we create a monochrome-camera recovery technique utilizing color image priors, resulting in improved restoration and refinement of single-channel images. We assess the performance of our methods on a variety of public datasets, and the results demonstrate their effectiveness and robustness, and the monochrome-camera technique outperforms existing methods, showcasing improved performance and reduced processing time.

Recent studies have revealed that certain simple systems with two degrees of freedom exhibit complex dynamical behavior. This paper focuses on the time-independent Hamiltonian of the Ermakov-Yukawa system. By constructing a Poisson bracket associated with this Hamiltonian, an associated dynamical system is formed, which exhibits characteristics of both regular and chaotic motion. Evidence for this complexity is demonstrated through the system's attractors in phase space and an analysis of its periodic orbits.

Research in Europe's public transportation reveals that buses are used in 50% of total trips. A major challenge in this sector is accurately forecasting passenger demand, as reliable data is often scarce. This study proposes a cutting-edge, non-invasive approach to gather transportation data by analyzing video feeds from buses, thereby boosting modeling capabilities. By comparing various methods for extracting data, we've discovered that comparing the positions of buses on routes is a reliable approach. Our analysis, conducted through a simulation, shows that this technique performs well, particularly when dealing with short transit routes, and is robust to variations in data collection frequency.

Recent advancements in few-shot learning have primarily focused on developing methods that utilize pre-trained models and employ task-adaptive adjustments to achieve accurate classifications using limited examples. This paper presents an alternative approach, which reformulates few-shot learning as a sequential prediction problem and utilizes the forward inference process from pre-trained models to derive features from the few-shot examples. The proposed framework, called FL-RL, is built upon reinforcement learning's Q-learning technique and has a mathematical equivalence to few-shot learning. Through experiments, the effectiveness of the proposed FL-SHOT framework is demonstrated on few-shot learning tasks, resulting in performance improvements over current state-of-the-art methods.

We're analyzing systems that are invariant under certain transformations, known as non-Abelian symmetries, with the aim of finding their corresponding non-invertible counterparts. A key example is the connection between chiral non-Abelian symmetry and the ADJ anomaly, which corresponds to a non-Abelian fusion category of gapped boundaries in a specific co-braided fusion category. A distinct non-Abelian fusion category with a non-trivial 3-cocycle invariant gives rise to another non-invertible symmetry termed the "charge symmetry." A general theory is proposed for similar "charge symmetries" in systems exhibiting invertible higher-form symmetries. Proposed systems with non-Abelian charges include certain gauge groups, theories with specific fusion rules, and certain quantum group theories.

A semi-transitive graph has no directed cycles and for any sequence of connections, a link between the first and last nodes in that sequence doesn't exist. Researchers, Chen, Huang, and Zhu explored semi-transitive orientation for path cover numbers and introduced the concept of path $k$-partite graphs - graphs that meet specific criteria based on path cover numbers and relationships between nodes. They found that certain path cover graphs, including split path cover graphs, can be characterized by their relationship between nodes, and characterized split path 2-cover graphs.

A cutting-edge approach utilizing a cutting-edge deep learning method, referred to as a convolutional recurrent neural network, has exhibited exceptional performance in discriminating tau decays hadronic in muon experiments. In this study, we introduce an upgraded dataset consisting of 10 distinct variables derived from an upgraded deep learning classifier. These variables were compiled from a comprehensive analysis of tau decays hadronic in CERN's Large Hadron Collider, and our results demonstrate that employing a cutting-edge deep learning method can significantly enhance the detection capabilities in search for rare or forbidden processes.

In the context of time-varying celestial events, such as those observed by the LIGO/Virgo gravitational wave detectors, distinguishing between different types of signals is crucial. We've developed a Bayesian Neural Network (BNN) classifier for this purpose, leveraging unlabeled data to enhance its effectiveness. Our study shows that this BNN achieves superior accuracy compared to traditional non-bayesian classifiers, and that incorporating unlabeled data further boosts its performance by around 5%. Furthermore, we've proven that the uncertainty estimates generated by the BNN are accurate, facilitating its use in real-time data processing. This is particularly relevant for applications such as parameter estimation and the detection of exotic compact objects, including boson stars, that may be present in the data.

Our study demonstrates the high efficiency of intermodal forward Brillouin scattering in solid-core photonic crystal fibers using the strong acoustic mode resonance at 110.32 MHz, achieving a 20.5 dB conversion gain and 2 mm coherence length through a 2100 rim-hole structure.

The concept of ordered generating sequences (OGS) extends a fundamental property of cyclic groups to non-cyclic groups. This ordered sequence, consisting of generators, effectively breaks down a group into a chain of subgroups, ultimately resulting in the group itself. In particular, for non-abelian groups, each group element can be uniquely represented through a distinct sequence of elements from the generating set. Given a fixed order of elements in the generating set, there exists a mapping that associates each group element with a sequence of lengths. This paper delves into a new property of OGS, specifically the distribution of sequence lengths. By calculating the first moments for both the symmetric group $S_3$ and a treelattice group of order 108, patterns emerge that enable the derivation of general formulas for the first moments in any group.

Two related, complex optimization challenges, known as the Set-Union Knapsack Problem and the Budgeted Maximum Coverage Problem, have been shown to be computationally difficult to solve optimally. Despite significant research, there has been a notable lack of efficient algorithms capable of delivering strong results within a reasonable time frame. We propose a new approach, called SETALGO, that provides a theoretical guarantee of at least 61% of the optimal solution within a polynomial time frame. By leveraging high-performance software packages and advanced search strategies, SETALGO is able to outperform existing solutions while providing a useful starting point for more in-depth local search. Our computational experiments demonstrate that SETALGO successfully delivers remarkable results on a wide range of test cases, breaking previous records for many instances where more sophisticated methods struggle.

Churn prevention in business is crucial for maintaining a profitable customer base.
This study focuses on predicting and analyzing churn in the online gambling industry.
To churn the operator from a game, our analysis examines whether new or existing customers close their accounts.
We applied a cutting-edge classification technique, utilizing a broad array of neural network architectures, and assessed their effectiveness using performance indicators such as AUC, Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1 Score.
Our results reveal that the ResNet model excelled with an AUC of 0.933, accuracy of 0.911, precision of 0.941, recall of 0.911, and F1 Score of 0.926, outperforming other models.
The ExNet, DxNet, SqueezeNet, and MobileNet models followed closely, achieving high performance scores across the board.
In contrast, the PoNNS model failed to reach acceptable levels, resulting in poor performance scores.
Our study's significance is threefold: it offers fresh insights into neural network performance in specific business applications, utilizes a unique dataset for the operator, and is the first to explore churning online gamblers within the business analytics field.

We have obtained the accurate complex critical exponents for Ising Field Theory at two specific points in the complex complex-cosine-Gordon coupling constant, the Yang-Lee edge singularity and the free fermion point. This was made possible by analyzing the singular behavior of the two-point function in Smirnov-Wilson momentum space up to 40th order using a computer algebra system. By cross-verifying results across coupled constants and physical observables using multiple independent methods, we determined that the observed patterns are well-supported by conformal field theory predictions. Furthermore, our research reveals that the leading edge singularity behavior corresponds to a unitary fixed point outside the unit circle, while other values result in non-unitary fixed points. This finding is in contrast to previous conjectures suggesting universal fixed points for all values.

Our research focuses on a specific type of process involving the polarization of gluons, which occurs in collisions of high-energy protons. By analyzing how gluons behave when they have transverse momentum, we developed a theoretical framework that helps us calculate this process. This framework involves a complex function, which describes how gluons are distributed within the proton, and our work has helped to refine this function through theoretical advancements in quantum chromodynamics. By applying this function to experimental data from large-scale studies of polarized proton collisions, we obtained precise measurements of how gluons behave in these interactions. Our results indicate that these polarized gluon interactions follow a specific pattern, which matches predictions made using simplified mathematical models, and also provides constraints on other potential interactions.

In the photon-photon interaction that occurs during ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, electron-positron pairs are produced through a process called the Bethe-Heitler reaction. When these collisions involve lead nuclei, relativistic contraction results in the formation of photon fields, which can be visualized as a spectrum of virtual photons. These virtual photons can then interact to create electron-positron pairs. To study this phenomenon, researchers have developed a simulation tool called \textsc{VPHITSnrel}, which calculates phase-space distributions of the photon spectrum, and subsequently, the space-time and momentum distributions of the resulting electron-positron pairs. The \textsc{VPHITSnrel} code has been tested and validated against existing results from Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC energy of 2.76 TeV, demonstrating its capability to investigate photon-photon collisions in ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions.

Evaluating cycling routes involves assessing factors like traffic, accident history, and personal preferences. This process is time-consuming and labor-intensive, requiring a thorough understanding of the terrain. We propose an innovative, practical, and efficient system that uses aerial imagery to automatically calculate the risk level of any given route. This image-based approach surpasses traditional methods in terms of speed and ease of implementation. The framework also tackles the challenge of finding the shortest route in complex road networks, where standard algorithms often fall short. To address this issue, we developed an efficient search strategy that integrates various cycling-related metrics, such as slope, curvature, and speed, to generate more realistic routing results. The risk assessment module further enhances the accuracy of the routing algorithm by tagging each road segment with real-time risk data. The integration of these components yields precise and optimized routes, outperforming existing alternatives. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this proposed system on a diverse set of geographical locations.

A new safety-critical method, known as "Algebraic Somatic Markov Decision Functions," combines Control Barrier Functions and Algebraic Somatic Markov Decision Functions to create "Summarized Safety-Dynamics Mappings." These mappings ensure that learned controllers are secure, efficient, and adaptable. By utilizing Algebraic Somatic Markov Decision Functions, related learned controllers can share knowledge and improve safety and efficiency. Our research demonstrates the feasibility of this approach and shows that related learned controllers exhibit similar secure and efficient behaviors.

A ring $R$ is classified as $\tau$-elementary if the covering number of $R$ equals the number of its nonzero two-sided ideals and $R/\Omega$ also exhibits the same property for a prime number $\tau$ and a particular ideal $\Omega$ of $R$.

Deep Neural Networks' susceptibility to adversarial inputs, which cause incorrect predictions, poses a significant issue. To rectify this, various regularization and adversarial training methods have been proposed, but they are often either imperfect or overly demanding. In contrast, Deep Neural Network robustness has been attributed to its capacity to withstand perturbations in training data. However, a hypothesis that Neural Networks inherently possess resistance to adversarial examples is yet to be thoroughly validated. In this research, we investigate Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (Neural ODEs), a deep learning framework, and demonstrate that their continuous nature inherently confers immunity against adversarial examples. Our study reveals that Neural ODEs naturally exhibit zero misclassification error on a widely-used benchmark dataset, the MNIST, without the need for supplementary techniques. Furthermore, we demonstrate that adding noise to adversarial examples fails to generate new, malicious examples. These findings suggest that Neural ODEs could serve as a promising avenue for developing more secure neural networks.

The nonlocal conservation laws for vehicular traffic are modeled using a kernel that accounts for the local and nonlocal interactions between vehicles in the lanes. This model's properties are analyzed in two-dimensional space with periodic boundaries. Existence and uniqueness of the model's solutions are proven for multiple lanes as well as two-dimensional space. Building upon the one-dimensional model, our analysis includes precise estimates on the properties of the model, particularly concerning the velocity term in the characteristic ordinary differential equations. Finally, by applying the Picard-Lindelof theorem, the model's solutions are established as globally existent.

Generalized from translation surfaces, dilation surfaces allow for the integration
of dilation operations. This introduces a directional flow that cannot occur on
translation surfaces alone. Focussing on a specific type of dilation surface that
involves a regular n-gon, we identify conditions allowing us to fully understand
the dilation patterns and thereby complete this analysis for all cases where n is
less than or equal to five.

Recent studies have suggested using total correlation to measure functional connectivity between brain regions, as it offers advantages over conventional methods by capturing and quantifying complex, complex-dependent relationships. This research aims to improve total correlation's feasibility for use in neuroscience by developing a new estimator, Total Correlation Deep Autoencoder (TCDE), which leverages deep autoencoders to achieve this goal. Furthermore, the corresponding optimization issue is formulated and solved using stochastic subgradient methods, showcasing the theoretical and practical benefits of TCDE. It is applied to real-world brain signal datasets to demonstrate its effectiveness and feasibility.

The classical Segal-Bargmann theory explores three key Hilbert space unitary 
isomorphisms that explain the dual nature of waves and particles, Hilbert space 
decompositions, and the dual interplay between position and momentum. This 
research generalizes these concepts to their quantum counterparts using q-deformed 
Segler-Bargmann theory's framework and provides necessary conditions for 
validating these theories in finite fields.

Gaussian processes (GP) serve as a versatile prior for regression and function optimization tasks, primarily due to their theoretical simplicity and effectiveness. Focusing on their posterior distributions, however, poses significant computational challenges, which are typically addressed through approximate methods like the Granger-Karhunen-Loeve expansion or stochastic approximation using Newton's method. In contrast, Monte Carlo methods, though capable of accurately representing GP posteriors, are hindered by slow convergence rates and the need to precompute a large number of samples, rendering them impractical for real-time applications. This research presents a novel approach, known as Fast Sampling, to streamline the Monte Carlo method's accuracy by iteratively refining sample quality through a process of fine-tuning. By leveraging a process known as stochastic gradient ascent, Fast Sampling achieves significant improvements in sampling efficiency, reducing it from an O(d^2) complexity to an almost linear complexity of O(d log d).

This research demonstrates that in outdoor settings with wireless communications employing antenna setups like the NS-2305 dipole, ground reflection plays a crucial role. Consequently, position estimation should consider and utilize this phenomenon by incorporating a two-path model that accounts for signal paths from the transmitter to receiver and also from transmitter to ground and then to receiver. Experimental results show that a Gaussian radial basis function neural network can accurately recover angle of arrival (AoA) and distance (SoD) using ground reflection, but relies on knowledge of the distance between receiver and transmitter. Conversely, a neural network can also derive distance from time of arrival (ToA) data obtained from ground reflection, but requires extensive training. Moreover, a novel two-step approach combining ground-based and ground-free position estimation has been introduced, utilizing ToA and AoD/AoA information, respectively, to calculate distance and angle/distance without mutual dependency.

The last few decades have been marked by significant progress in understanding the behavior of neutrinos.  This area of study has led to the development of a new field of research.  Over a century ago, physicists Pauli and Fermi initially proposed the existence of neutrinos.  It was later confirmed by experiments, particularly the one conducted at Mount Washington in 1956.  Since then, researchers have continuously studied the behavior of neutrinos and found evidence of their transformation between different states.  This paper focuses on the changes in neutrino states, the changes in their mass, and the experimental results related to these phenomena, highlighting the significance of neutrino research in cosmology and particle physics.

Research on top quarks and pairs has emerged as a key area in exploring physics that goes beyond the standard model, with top quarks offering significant potential in this regard. Although current data from the ATLAS and CMS experiments at the LHC has not yet provided definitive signs of new physics, it is expected to do so with increased luminosity data, specifically 300 fb^-1 at 13 TeV, which will be covered in upcoming searches. With the upcoming High-Luminosity LHC, researchers will be able to test even more complex and detailed theories. This article details the current status of the top quark and beyond-the-standard-model searches at the LHC and outlines future prospects.
