In clinical trials, repeated measures using mixed models often face limitations due to treating time as a categorical variable. While using numerical time as a continuous variable mitigates some issues, it also comes with its own drawbacks. To address these concerns, we've developed a new method for modeling time using real-valued functions within a numerical model. This novel approach allows the treatment effect on the slope of the response to be flexible, rather than being constrained by continuous models designed for time-to-event outcomes. A key advantage is the development of model testing procedures for treating time as continuous, providing more accurate model fits. We've successfully applied this approach to model numerical covariates in repeated measures trials.

A novel computational method called Action-based On-Surface Hybrid DFT is introduced to analyze complex molecular structures. This method assesses a smooth potential energy function derived from a reaction pathway, which is then used to approximate the Onsager-Machlup action and identify key features such as transition states and reaction barriers without relying on density functional theory energy calculations. The effectiveness of this method is tested on a variety of DFT energy surfaces and molecular systems, including adenine and benzene, which demonstrates its potential to calculate precise reaction pathways and energy barriers for these structures. This method is expected to be highly efficient and scalable, allowing it to tackle large systems with minimal computational cost.

This study focuses on obtaining L-infinity estimates for a particular class of parabolic equations of complex Monge-Ampere type, utilizing alternative approaches that can be easily adapted between different models. Additionally, it explores a discrete variant of the equation, which enables for the development of a L-infinity model mean curvature flow. The results obtained in this research have implications for the study of flow by curvature in an infinite horizon setting.

Building on the circuit complexity model, this study focuses on the automata theory, and we establish that the class of polyregular functions constitutes precisely the polymorphic time-constructible functions. Furthermore, the result indicates that for each individual function within this class, a corresponding automaton exists, capable of computing the function's value within polynomial time. To achieve this, we develop novel techniques in computational complexity, specifically the study of polynomial-time evaluation of functions and their representations, and we delve into the intricacies of the involved mathematical and algorithmic concepts. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that the previously open question of the polyregular functions' closure properties can be resolved, and we show that they indeed form a closed class under composition. Additionally, we provide characterizations of the sub-classes within this category, and we discuss their relationships to the broader hierarchy of the Sch\"{u}nhofier-Amer classification.

This concise note establishes a relationship between Ito and Stratonovich integrals when conditional measure flow components are involved in the integrands, with the 'correction' term requiring consideration of Lions-type measure flows. It demonstrates that this 'correction' term is generally non-zero, with specific conditions under which it becomes non-zero explicitly stated. This note assumes a common background of stochastic calculus and optimal control theory, with the exception of the exceptional treatment of conditional measure flows.

This study aims to investigate various types of normal subgroups using a specific topology defined by Shahabi and Ebrahimi. We will demonstrate that the set of all normal subgroups of a group does not generally form a group under a specific operation, with the exception of abelian groups. We will also explore topological properties and introduce a new class of normal subgroups.

This study addresses the challenge of generating SQL queries in text that comes from multiple domains. The proposed method, based on the observation that several key factors contribute to its success, includes leveraging a shared SQL vocabulary across domains, combining insights from both single and multi-domain training data, and combining generated SQL queries to improve their quality. The results show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on a critical single-domain evaluation benchmark and also performs well in a critical multi-domain evaluation benchmark.

In complex multi-robot systems, accurately navigating a single robot amidst obstacles and uncertain factors is a significant challenge, particularly when dealing with limited and unreliable sensor data. Our method addresses this issue by incorporating distributionally robust conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) measures into the local planning algorithm of each robot. By calculating online optimal controls based on obstacle avoidance constraints, our approach calculates a risk-averse CVaR for each degree of freedom, ensuring robustness against uncertain obstacle positions and sensor errors. Analytically derived obstructions are sampled, allowing for a computationally efficient calculation of CVaR without the need for computationally intensive sampling methods. Our proposed approach can be applied to various motion planning techniques that employ point-wise constraints, and our results demonstrate a significant reduction in path planning failures, even under severe uncertainty conditions.

Recent research has suggested that ultra-diffuse Andromeda dwarf galaxies (uAndromeda galaxies) may be predominantly composed of old, low-mass stars. However, a key aspect of this hypothesis remains unexplored: the presence of interstellar gas. In an effort to examine this possibility, we have employed the ALMA telescope to observe three uAndromeda galaxies - Andromeda XXV, XXVI, and XXVII - in a search for gas. Our observations reveal that Andromeda XXV possesses a systemic velocity of approximately -269 km/s and no detectable gas emission above the sensitivity threshold. In contrast, our findings for Andromeda XXVI and XXVII reveal low-mass, single-component gas masses of around 10^5 to 10^6 solar masses, with low gas fractions of approximately 0.001. Although our observations confirm that uAndromeda galaxies do contain gas, its mass is too low to be the primary constituent. Consequently, our results imply that previous assumptions regarding the existence of gas-rich uAndromeda galaxies as the progenitors of uDwarf galaxies are likely inaccurate.

In massive machine-type communications, grant-free access offers a scalable and low-latency solution by eliminating random access procedures. However, uncertainty arises from unconfirmed transmissions affecting system performance. Research has addressed this challenge through grant-free designs, such as grant-free radar, which minimizes interference and enhances detection capabilities, yet traditional approaches do not fully leverage the joint transmission-reflection capabilities of joint communication-radar systems, nor do they resolve the grant-free access dilemma. This paper introduces a novel framework, joint grant-free communication-radar, which optimizes radar performance and reliability in a low-latency setup. The proposed framework iteratively decomposes the joint optimization problem into sub-problems, and employs techniques like block-dictionary learning, to simplify complexity and enhance robustness. In comparison to sequential approaches, experimental results demonstrate the proposed framework's superior performance in enhanced radar, improved system reliability, and optimal system balance.
A general framework for thermodynamics of moist air is presented, utilizing various thermodynamic potentials and emphasizing the specific internal energy formulation.

We introduce algebraic objects, which generalise ordered semirings and monoids, and extend the concept of semirings and monoids by adding an additional element. In this new structure, the added element accounts for inequalities such as a ≥ 0 and a ≤ 0 simultaneously. An algebra with this unique property is denoted as a "doubled semirring" or "ds-ring". In ds-rings, traditional identities like a ≥ b ≥ c and a ≥ c ≥ b are equivalent. Building on this idea, further generalisation leads to the concept of "F1 ds-rings" or "F1 double category", which encompasses all possible instances of Grothendieck's categories with divisors when reduced to integers. Specifically, ds-rings exhibit characteristics of both a monoid and an antimonoid, allowing the application of monoid and category theory to the study of algebraic structures, including factorisation theory and the theory of monoids with divisors. Notably, certain ds-rings, such as F-valued function semirings, exhibit applications in coding and cryptography through the use of metric spaces.

This study explores the feasibility of spoken dialogue systems (SDS) based on confusion networks (CNs) instead of traditional top-N ASR hypotheses. The central premise of the CN approach is that it leverages diverse, yet plausible ASR outcomes to enhance interaction handling in the system. The CN-SDS architecture demonstrates superior performance compared to a baseline model utilizing the top-N hypotheses directly, thanks to its capacity to model relationships between related hypotheses and access a broader range of hypotheses. Furthermore, the CN-CDS SDS and logit selector selectors also surpass their non-CN counterparts.

We introduce new ways of quantifying semistable coherent sheaves on complex curves through modifications of existing enumerative invariants, specifically by dividing a standard sheaf invariants by those of curves that fail to be of full rank. This process yields novel invariants, such as modified versions of homological invariants like Euler and Poincaré series, along with variational formulas and integrability conditions that extend existing results. In the context of a complex projective curve, we establish an integrability-based integration formula that integrates basic invariants across all curve dimensions, which in turn facilitates computations of basic invariants through integration methods, including integration over moduli spaces of curves. Additionally, we apply our integration formula to derive an expression of basic invariants as a modified version of homological invariants, specifically by integrating modified invariants over curves of full rank.

A critical factor in secret sharing schemes is the count of minimal qualified subsets, specifically those with a size of $n$ in a $(k,n)$-scheme. The universal access structure, denoted as $\Delta_{max}$, is characterized by every subset of $[n]$ having a non-empty intersection with some qualified subset. This study presents lower and upper bounds for the count of minimal qualified subsets in $\Delta_{max}$ and demonstrates that for $k \ge 2$, there exist access structures within $\Delta_{max}$ that are not realizable through any secret sharing scheme, with the only exception being $(k-1,n)$-schemes which are indeed realizable within $\Delta_{max}$.

We've found the most accurate approach for determining the entanglement of polarization qubits by measuring polarization-related observables. Our method not only yields the optimal precision limit for estimating entanglement under specific conditions but also helps us to calculate specific precision limits dependent on parameters like photon number and visibility for specific families of states, demonstrating that product states can achieve high accuracy in estimating entanglement under certain visibility ranges.

The study of non-linear coherent structures in plasma is an emerging area of research. These formations, including magnetic islands and current sheets, transport parallel currents and play a crucial role in plasma transport and energy dissipation through reconnection processes. These structures, referred to as Current Sheet Structures (CSs), emerge from the non-linear interaction of linearly unstable Alfv\'{e}n waves and the drift of ions, and are characterized by the formation of magnetic islands and current sheets. A theoretical framework for simulating these structures is presented, and their properties are studied through numerical modeling. The simulations reveal a variety of CS shapes, sizes, and velocities, and their stability is examined. The potential implications of these CSs for plasma transport and reconnection processes are discussed.

Frozen-pretrained models have achieved remarkable success in various tasks. Nonetheless, they have been underutilized for Continual Learning (CL), where images of different categories need to be learned incrementally. By leveraging a frozen-pretrained model, CL challenges can be tackled more effectively, as data retrieval is not necessary. We introduce CL-FP, an approach utilizing a frozen-pretrained model without the need for additional modifications. Initially, an existing CL-FP implementation is critiqued, highlighting its key limitations. Our approach offers two key benefits over these limitations. Firstly, we substitute the existing feature extractor with a more effective one. Secondly, we introduce a new unsupervised method that correctes decision boundaries, enhancing the performance of the existing model. Our experiments confirm that these enhancements significantly elevate the performance of the baseline model.

As social media platforms grow, so does the issue of hate speech online, which can lead to severe consequences such as mental illness and physical violence. While technology can't prevent the occurrence of hate speech, it can help mitigate its impact by providing filtering and detection capabilities. This research focuses specifically on detecting hate speech in Hindi tweets, an underdeveloped area in NLP. The study involves a detailed analysis of tweets labeled as non-hate, offensive but not hateful, and hate speech, which were collected through crowdsourcing. The results showed that the best results were achieved using BERT, with a precision of 77.4%, recall of 74.2%, and a F1 score of 75.8%.

We introduce and investigate the traveling wave method for efficiently simulating large networks of identical and similar neural models. This method involves solving a partial differential equation to a solution that approximates the neural model, and it outperforms traditional integrators by a factor of hundreds of times. Notably, the proposed method exhibits improved performance when applied to random networks with varying in-degree distributions, specifically showing reduced oscillations in networks with a wider distribution. Furthermore, the method yields a continuous solution that provides insights into collective dynamics in neural networks, and it can be extended to networks of graph Laplacians to model more complex neural systems.

Recent years have seen the application of various neural network-based methods in program repair. One of these is Generative Adversial Network, which is typically used to create high-quality, realistic images. Our research introduces a novel approach to using GAN for automatically repairing source code, where the discriminator network is trained to recognize correctly and incorrectly modified programs, and GAN enables the generation of multiple potential fixes for a single input program. We have implemented and tested this method for C and Java languages, comparing its results to other machine learning-based program repair methods and finding that it performs comparably to them.

This study introduces a capacity formula for a broad category of interference channels, encompassing both discrete and continuous variables, by utilizing spectral mutual information rates. For this channel class, the level of noise and a specific function related to the noise are considered as random, with their average levels governed by a given noise profile. By applying a spectral mutual information rate definition that correlates with interference channel inputs and the noise profile, we derive a capacity formula involving these rates. Furthermore, we prove the existence and expressibility of optimal time and frequency allocations in terms of these rates, which maximize the sum of power and channel gains, and demonstrate that this solution yields the sum capacity region. Numerical examples are used to illustrate a sum capacity formula for a Gaussian interference channel with correlated noise, confirming that this formula exceeds an existing outer bound.

We're investigating the influence of various nuclear collision models, including eALEPPO and GiBUU, which have a semi-classical nature. These models are being compared to a dynamic equation of state-based model, and it's found that they exhibit different behavior regarding flow coefficients and nuclear matter compression. Notably, it's discovered that there are multiple variations of the dynamic equation of state-based model depending on how they handle nucleon mean fields, and this has significant implications for understanding nuclear collision outcomes. It's also found that incorporating baryon mean fields into these models can have substantial effects on nuclear collision outcomes, which highlights the importance of examining this factor in other model types. Ultimately, it's concluded that it's crucial to compare various models with each other in order to effectively assess their strengths and weaknesses in simulating nuclear collisions.

The rapid spread of the COVID-19 pandemic has led to a surge in global mortality rates, with healthcare systems overwhelmed by the sheer number of cases. To address this challenge, it is crucial to identify and isolate infected individuals early on to prevent further transmission. To this end, researchers have developed various machine learning models capable of detecting the disease through laboratory testing methods such as RT-PCR, but these methods are time-consuming. To bridge this gap, a novel deep learning model based on a modified residual neural network has been proposed to analyze chest X-ray images and predict COVID-19 cases. By incorporating attention mechanisms into a CNN-RNN framework, this model can focus on and learn from the most significant features within chest X-ray images. Evaluating its performance using a publicly available dataset, the results show that this model achieves exceptional accuracy in correctly classifying COVID-19 cases, significantly outperforming existing models in terms of its area under the receiver operating characteristic curve.

A graph neural network (GNN) has seen significant success in the field of wireless communication. However, the complexity of its design and the challenges posed by its non-convex nature have led to several problems, such as the difficulty in replicating or adapting a given GNN to other scenarios. To address these issues, we have developed a practical framework for translating and adapting advanced GNNs designed for specific tasks in wireless communication to other GNN-based systems.

significant percentage of the country's total mortality rate.
Black individuals have the highest homicide rate, but they also face significant
barriers in accessing justice system information due to a lack of detailed
documentation in Brazil's judicial system.
This research presents a system that uses natural language processing to extract
and aggregate specific information from individual homicide court documents,
focusing on demographic attributes.
By utilizing an unsupervised model to detect specialized terminology and a
supervised deep learning model to identify personal attributes, the proposed
method is capable of extracting key information from document excerpts.
This system has been tested on a dataset of 100,000 excerpts from court documents
covering 6 cities in Brazil and has achieved an overall accuracy of 84.2%.
The system has been applied to a dataset of 1.2 million individuals from the same
collection of court documents, revealing that the extracted demographic
information is correct in 87.9% of the cases.

actionable insights to address this disparity by linking individual cases to a larger
database.

We investigate how stochastic gradient descent converges in our optimization experiments. Specifically, we focus on minimizing smooth, strongly-convex functions in $\mathbb{R}^d$ using stochastic gradient descent with an exponentially decreasing step size. This study is the first of its kind to provide a convergence rate for this combination of parameters. Our results show that an exponentially decreasing step size of order $1/k$ in stochastic gradient descent leads to a convergence rate of $\exp(-\kappa T)$ in this process. This is achieved by proving that the distance to the optimal solution is bounded in expectation by this distance at the start. Our proof is based on a new approach that involves decomposing the distance to the optimal solution into two martingale terms. This study also discusses the implications of our findings on other optimization methods, such as accelerated gradient descent and stochastic accelerated methods.

Axion and Axion-Like Particles (ALPs) emerge as byproducts of several key breakthroughs in theoretical physics.  One notable discovery is that certain groups, such as $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z})$, act as symmetries in specific physics theories, resulting in non-trivial cocycles that give rise to ALPs.  This phenomenon occurs naturally in various physics models, including those addressing fundamental problems, such as the strong-CP issue.  In this context, we explore a theory called fractional T-duality, which has previously been studied in the context of gerbes, and our analysis reveals that fractional T-duality acts as a symmetry in a modified version of string theory.  This modified symmetry group, which includes $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z})$, acts on the target space of string theory, and the associated charge arises from a non-trivial $\mathbb{Z}_m$-valued 2-cocycle in group cohomology theory.  This particular 2-cocycle has been previously identified by others, including the second author, and our findings demonstrate its relevance in physics models.  Additionally, the modified symmetry group, which includes both conventional and fractional T-duality, has implications for mirror symmetry in string theory, as it enables us to express dualities in terms of algebraic equations rather than differential equations.

The ability to store information is fundamental to living organisms and is linked to complex processes occurring out of equilibrium. Currently, there isn't a clear understanding of the physical properties that enable the storage and processing of information. We suggest that the thermodynamic driving force behind a system's fluctuation-dissipation balance, known as the extended fluctuation-dissipation theorem's excess temperature, can serve as a measure of information storage capacity. We demonstrate this by utilizing spintronics as an example of how information can be temporarily held and manipulated by rapidly adjusting an system's ability to dissipate energy, thereby creating self-sustaining oscillations. This approach may provide a new perspective on information storage and open up possibilities for developing more efficient self-oscillating information processors.

Dexterous grasping in robotics is a complex challenge, compounded by a lack of comprehensive datasets that cover various objects and different control approaches. To address this issue, DexGraspNet has been created, a massive dataset consisting of over 1.5 million frames featuring more than 110,000 objects and 100,000 partial sequences. This dataset is designed to support dexterous grasping with two-fingered grippers and includes several unique characteristics such as diverse real-world scenarios and various optimization objectives. DexGraspNet is a collaborative effort, involving extensive research and development, and is available for download at https://dexterous-grasping.vision/ with various file formats and object-related information. DexGraspNet also includes a powerful 250GB visualizer that allows users to explore the dataset in a user-friendly manner. DexGraspNet is accompanied by a powerful foundation model that is trained on the entire dataset, and can generate samples for unseen objects up to 60 times per second on a single GPU, thus providing a unique opportunity to accelerate research in dexterous grasping and manipulation.

A novel approach is suggested to create and optimize a respiratory motion compensation algorithm for MRI scans. This method involves developing a patient-specific ventilation model using initial MRI data and implementing an optimization technique that utilizes proton density-maps from cardiac-gated MRI to complete and stabilize high-resolution images acquired throughout the respiratory cycle. Each incomplete set of data corresponds to a specific moment during the patient's breathing pattern. By leveraging this information, the proposed algorithm seeks to create accurate, high-resolution images for each respiratory step. This approach was applied to MRI scans of six human subjects, demonstrating improved agreement between model predictions and actual MRI data compared to conventional methods.

We introduce a novel approach to model compression, referred to as Stochastic Knowledge Distillation, which integrates the concepts of knowledge distillation and Monte Carlo dropout, and incorporates stochastic sampling during training. The proposed method enables the use of an uncompressed stochastic teacher model, and leverages dropout samples to approximate Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimates in the process of knowledge distillation. The framework incorporates an efficient, optimized training procedure, and our experimental results demonstrate significant performance improvements over existing techniques such as stochastic neural architecture search, pruning, quantization, and conventional knowledge distillation.

Two submersion functions from the set of two-dimensional real numbers to the set of real numbers are defined, and it is stated that they are topologically equivalent if and only if their respective foliations by curves are transversely topologically orderable. Transverse ordering is explained as being achievable through a continuous function that maps orbits to orbits. Additionally, we establish a method of classifying these functions based on their transverse ordering capabilities and relate this to their 1-dimensional homology characteristics.

Ecosystems with sparse vegetation are particularly vulnerable to degradation, especially those subjected to grazing. To understand how vegetation patterns respond to grazing pressure, researchers employed the SIMEVEG model, which incorporates multiple ecological processes driving pattern emergence. Focusing on the effect of grazing intensity on vegetation, scientists analyzed simulations from different spatial configurations and scaling laws and found that uneven plant distribution leads to more intense grazing than uniform arrangements do. Surprisingly, scaling laws exhibited minimal variation in this effect. Consequently, grazing simulations with low plant distribution and homogeneous distributions produced similar outcomes, suggesting that grazing pressure might be the primary factor in determining the stability of oscillating periodic patterns in these ecosystems.

A well-established dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch is utilized to map high-dimensional data vectors into a significantly lower dimension space. This technique allows the approximate computation of dominant properties such as the Lp norm and top-k Lp norms on vectors. However, it's worth noting that the dominant term in the error rate calculation,  $O(\frac{k\log n}{\varepsilon^p})$, is extremely large, making it impractical for computations. Our goal is to design a simpler and more efficient algorithm that can accurately estimate Lp norms on data vectors. The proposed solution involves a distributed algorithm that can be applied in both distributed and single-machine settings and is capable of computing an accurate estimation of the Lp norm of a vector with a polynomial number of samples. The algorithm is also designed to handle the computation of top-k Lp norms in a distributed environment and comes with theoretical guarantees regarding its accuracy.

A python-based program, auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo in action, demonstrates its capabilities with significant computational efficiency enhancements, particularly in its performance on a grid. Upgrades to the algorithm and a grid-centric approach to dimensionality have led to considerable speedups, specifically a notable 125x acceleration compared to its previous counterpart. This improvement holds across both single and multi-core environments, and speed gains are even more pronounced with an increase in the number of cores utilized. Additionally, the code's flexibility is showcased through its application to a variety of systems, encompassing Au and H2, with outcomes verified against established wavefunction theory benchmarks and auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo references. Potential uses of this new approach are illustrated through calculations of periodic Au and non-periodic CH4.

High-frequency trading algorithms have gained prominence in the financial sector, 
with the most successful ones adhering to game-theoretic principles. Notably, 
research indicates a shift toward game-theoretic and artificial-intelligence-based 
approaches, as the most effective PnL generators are often the result of a 
game-theoretic equilibrium. The concept of game-theoretic equilibrium implies 
continual adaptation and evolution, with successful algorithms evolving into a 
state of stability. However, once an algorithm reaches this equilibrium, its 
future performance becomes uncertain, with the most successful ones potentially 
declining. Our research proposes a high-frequency trading algorithm, based on 
the principles of artificial intelligence, and demonstrates its PnL generation 
through a simulated market based on an existing algorithm. Our simulated 
results suggest that the proposed algorithm exhibits characteristics of 
continuous improvement and stability, with our model approaching the state of 
optimal efficiency.

We examine a digital goods auction where buyers compete for $k$ identical items. Each buyer has a private valuation, modeled after a geometric distribution based on the expected number of users a company targeting the buyer will have in the future. For simplicity, we focus on items with identical distributions and no correlation between buyers. Given these assumptions, we established that finding the optimal revenue is an NP-hard problem, even when limiting the search to three items of the same type, under widely accepted complexity hypotheses. However, we found that when dealing with distinct items, the problem remains tractable even for ten items of diverse types, as solving the corresponding linear program suffices. Our study also extends to discrete generalization of continuous distributions, where valuations follow uniform distributions on integers. We found that the former and latter scenarios often yield similar revenue solutions.

A new system has been developed for abstractive summarization, which integrates a fixed-generate model with a mechanism for enhancing details through the integration of entity-based information. This mechanism, called an entity chain, acts as a "search query" for more specific information and allows for flexible applications such as anti-hallucination in summary generation. Through experiments conducted on two datasets, including XSum and crowdSum, results show that the proposed method successfully improves both sentence structure and information specificity in generated summaries, and on a dataset challenge called the CHyME, it demonstrated on par performance with strong baseline models for summarization tasks.

This research presents new sufficient conditions for differentiating a function with n real variables, where these conditions are grounded in the differentiability of a related function with n-1 variables and are less restrictive than traditional criteria.

Human vocal synchronization in social interactions provides valuable information about a person's cognitive behavior, enabling the estimation of cognitive-behavioral traits from their entrainment patterns. Existing methods for estimating entrainment in social conversations often fall short in accurately capturing complex interactions. To address this limitation, we introduce a new approach for pinpointing specific moments of synchronized speech production in conversational exchanges. By modeling entrainment as the conjunction of similarity and reciprocity, our technique identifies instances where speakers alternate producing matching tones. A novel algorithm is developed to calculate the entry and excursion of pitch distributions. Applying our method to a sound recording of a conversation with a medical doctor enabled us to identify moments of synchronized speech in the conversation. Analysis revealed that segments of synchronized speech are more prevalent in the conversation when compared to a control scenario. Furthermore, our evaluation of our method's accuracy in identifying moments of synchronized speech in the conversation showed that our technique effectively captures the entry and excursion of pitch, and our results align with human perceptions of the conversation. Based on the established connection between pitch-alternation similarity and cognitive behavior, our method can be utilized to estimate cognitive-behavioral traits in the conversation. A preliminary application of our method revealed that our analysis is consistent with established clinical assessments of the conversation.

A recent study applied a realizability technique to establish the meaning of a quantum lambda calculus, which results in a proof of its consistency, in particular, that free theorems do not arise within this system.

Calculations of quasiparticle excitations and localization lengths are carried out in a two-dimensional electron system using a semi-classical approach. The systems are based on a high magnetic field and a small number of electrons, and the calculations are performed using a 2D harmonic oscillator as a potential. Two models, the Laughlin theory and composite fermions theory, are used to perform variational calculations. The results are compared to experimentally measured quasiparticle excitation energies and localization lengths, and a comparison is also made with Digital Quantum Simulations. The results from both models are found to be in good agreement with experiment and DQS.

In this work, a finite element approach is developed to solve a specific type of variational inequality that incorporates non-smooth, non-symmetric constraints typical in glaciological problems. This approach involves constructing and analyzing a finite element scheme for a generalized Stokes problem subject to variational inequalities. This model accounts for two key phenomena: basal sliding of ice under certain conditions and the formation of ice cliffs due to cracking. For a particular finite element scheme, existence and uniqueness of constrained solutions are proven for a particular class of polygonal domains. Additionally, numerical results from a simulation for a real-world scenario, such as the Simunle glacier in China, demonstrate the significant impact of a phenomenon called ice cliff on glacier dynamics.

The interplay between a galaxy's star formation rate and its mass loss rate is a key factor in understanding how galaxies grow and form stars. This study investigates the relationship between outflow mass loss rates and other galaxy characteristics in 18 star-forming galaxies from the X-Shine sample. By combining data from multiple wavelengths and utilizing a sophisticated analysis technique, the researchers found that the outflow mass loss rates they measured are consistent across different redshifts and align with predictions based on a galaxy's star formation rate. This discovery confirms the significance of outflows in regulating galaxy growth over a wide range of star-forming conditions. Moreover, the results indicate that the energy output from outflows and the kinetic energy of star formation scale in a similar manner, suggesting that both the outflow mass loss rates and kinetic energy measurements accurately represent the energy output of outflows driven by different levels of a galaxy's star formation rate. This implies that the galaxy's star formation rate is the primary factor in determining the energy output of outflows.

Our research examined the connection between initial conditions and hydrodynamic evolution in order to unravel the underlying principles of initial state geometry and its influence on final-state properties observed in heavy ion collisions. We investigated the relationship between initial density fluctuations and final-state particle density observed in experimental measurements, along with an analysis of how different variables such as multiplicity and transverse momentum correlate with each other. We discovered that the relationship between initial density fluctuations and final-state particle density exhibits a clear correlation, suggesting that it may serve as a reliable indicator of initial state geometry evolution. Furthermore, our analysis revealed that when accounting for the effects of transverse momentum, it becomes possible to distinguish between different types of initial state geometry fluctuations, ultimately revealing a more nuanced understanding of how initial state geometry influences final-state particle density.

This paper presents a novel swarm system architecture, dubbed Robotic Swarm System (RSS), which facilitates a robotic swarm's collaborative and coordinated efforts. An RSS framework is established to synchronize robotic movements through a transparent, real-time system-wide notification and warning mechanism. This architecture allows an autonomous entity to initiate changes to the system's state and disseminate system-wide notifications and warnings in real-time. Consequently, all participating robots can assess information related to movement initiation, progression, and completion, enabling them to execute maneuvers safely and coordinate with others. The proposed architecture supports multiple concurrent notifications and warnings with varying priority levels and provides a transparent mechanism to assess the relevance of received notifications and warnings. The effectiveness of RSS is demonstrated through case studies, including a simulated car racing scenario and a real-world car racing trial.

A novel approach utilizes depth maps extracted from unmarked videos to generate supplementary training data for DNNs, thus enhancing their training efficiency. The method employs transfer learning, where DNNs are initially trained on large datasets, followed by training on damped data, which is generated using the self-supervised depth estimation technique and a boundary loss function. The boundary loss is utilized to prevent inaccurate depth predictions, which are then leveraged to create robust training data. The integration of this self-generated data significantly boosts the performance of DNNs in the challenging task of semantic segmentation, particularly when dealing with real-world scenes. The proposed approach is further demonstrated to produce superior semantic segmentation outcomes, which are validated through experiments conducted on the Cityscapes dataset. The associated code and models can be accessed at https://github.com/ashishkumar1999/deepselftrain.

Bohr's inequality provides a minimum threshold $\delta$ for the variable $r$ such that each term $a_nz^n$ in the power series satisfies the bound $|a_nz^n|\leq r$, and this $\delta$ has a known optimal value. The original $\delta$ was determined to be $\frac13$, but it was later found that incorporating the series' sum into the bound $|\sum a_nz^n|\leq 1$ results in a narrower Bohr radius, which was initially found in works by Ralevic and Singh, and others. This paper aims to further explore this finding, and also introduces a novel concept of reduced $\delta$ for the modified bound. This new reduced $\delta$ was first identified in works by Aulaskanta and Pathak. Here, we present specific conditions under which the reduced $\delta$ is identified, and also introduce a general result that identifies optimal $\delta$ for the difference $|\sum a_nz^n|-1|$, which was first introduced in works by Aulaskanta and Raut, and later generalized. This paper also introduces a general result that identifies reduced $\delta$ for the sum of the series' bound and the distance from the unit disk $|\sum a_nz^n|-1|+\eta(r)$, which was first introduced in works by Aulaskanta and Raut, and later generalized. This new reduced $\delta$ was first identified in works by

A nonparametric measure of correlation known as Kendall's tau is being used to correlate ranked data. It remains one of the most popular measures due to its simplicity and robustness. However, traditional calculations involve a time-consuming O(n^2) procedure. A recent advancement proposed a faster O(nlogn) estimation method, but it was found to provide biased results. We present a revised estimate with the same O(nlogn) efficiency but without bias. Furthermore, a new hypothesis test based on this revised estimate offers enhanced statistical power. We demonstrate through simulations that our revised method and test outperform their counterparts in calibrated power. Ultimately, we apply our new approach to a real-world dataset involving over 100,000 participants in a genetic association study.

A next-generation transportation system, known as Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS), incorporates a range of sensors to monitor and track vehicles and road conditions. However, its current infrastructure-based design is constrained by issues of latency, privacy, and reliability. To address these shortcomings, we propose the concept of Edge Intelligence Systems (EIS) to support ITS through a distributed and intelligent computing framework. By empowering edge devices with advanced artificial intelligence capabilities, such as data processing, device management, and service orchestration. This paper delves into the key technologies that will enable EIS to operate within ITS, including machine learning, cloud computing, and device management. Additionally, we identify critical research challenges that need to be overcome to fully realize the potential of EIS in ITS applications.

This study focuses on the application of the Euler characteristic for specific types of set-valued mappings, including multi-valued maps and hypergraphs, extending previous research. Additionally, a new concept of homological index for Valued Graphs is introduced and investigated.

Our analysis focuses on an adjusted predator-prey model with a complex type of effect known as double Holling allee, incorporating random disturbances, leading to a stochastic system on a defined spatial area. This novel model offers insights into how population densities of prey and predator behave over time, showcasing coexistence and extinction scenarios across different parameter values. Additionally, we provide a precise mathematical description of how the model's outcomes change with varying environmental conditions, known as stationary distribution.

The Hirsch Conjecture proposed a relationship between the number of facets of a d-dimensional polytope and its diameter, which is a measure of the longest path between any two vertices. This relationship, however, was disproven by Santos in 2014 with a specific example of a polytope in which the number of vertices far exceeded the number of facets of a certain type of polytope. In order to understand the validity of the Hirsch Conjecture, researchers began by studying simplified versions of the problem in which the edges of the polytope satisfied certain geometric conditions, which are a more restrictive form. This paper further narrows the geometric conditions on the edges and proves that under these conditions, a certain relationship holds for all simplicial polytopes, which are a specific type of polytope. This result closely mirrors the original Hirsch Conjecture and closely relates to a more recent study that provided similar results for cyclic polytopes, which are a specific type of polytope in a higher dimensional space.

We explore in an associative ring R with identity, the scarcity of k-torsion in the NK1Q(R), where k is a positive integer, k divides no number of the form ab+a+-a, where a varies from 1 to k and b is any element in R, and a, b are not invertible. To achieve this goal, we compute R's nilpotency degree D of RNkQ over RNQ for the local ring R, and the nilpotency degree DkQ over Dk-1Q for the ring DkQ over Dk-1Q, where DkQ over Dk-1Q is considered a DKQ-Dk-1Q module.

This paper undertakes a thorough comparison of the comprehensive, off-shell computation for J/psi decaying into the muon pair and other channels, primarily to evaluate precise off-shell and non-resonant inputs crucial for the coherent J/psi production in Coulomb-nuclear interference experiments. Utilizing the same numerical framework, our analysis encompasses not only the primary channel but also contributions from gamma and cobarbeta particles as well as other channels involving chirality flips, resulting in precise predictions for the interference pattern. Our code accurately accounts for off-shell effects and provides numerical estimates for their magnitude.

The susceptibility of facial recognition systems to fraudulent activities poses a significant threat to safety-critical uses. To counter this, researchers have proposed methods to assess the authenticity of live subjects during face authentication processes. A novel approach has been developed that enables real-time, on-device verification of live subjects using depth data and neural networks. This proposed method demonstrates enhanced accuracy, surpassing existing techniques in performance metrics of true positive rates while maintaining depth detection sensitivity and overall depth data availability during testing.

In the realm of autonomous vehicles, supervised learning has been a prominent approach despite its inherent challenge – acquiring vast amounts of labeled data proves costly and time-consuming due to the necessity for accurate annotations. To alleviate this issue, this study proposes an innovative framework called Curriculum Learning for Annotating Driving Scenarios (CLAD), which aims to pinpoint the most beneficial frames requiring expert labeling. By leveraging an annotation acquisition policy, CLAD determines which frames should be prioritized for human annotation, thereby optimizing the labeling process. Furthermore, CLAD incorporates a curriculum learning strategy, where the annotation policy evolves iteratively based on the vehicle's progress through a driving simulation task. Through the application of a deep neural network model for vehicle classification in a simulated urban driving environment, CLAD demonstrates significant improvements over traditional methods of labeling, achieving accurate vehicle classification rates of 80.4% while reducing the necessary labeled samples by 20.8% compared to a baseline approach.

Evolutionary algorithms have been applied across diverse fields, but their performance variability poses a problem for online searches. While recent studies have attempted to mitigate this, most approaches are based on batch evaluations. Our research investigates the bias in evaluation time due to task-dependent computation costs in evolutionary algorithms. Through theoretical analysis and numerical simulations, we demonstrate that standard methods like increasing population size or reducing parallel task execution do not effectively reduce performance differences. Our findings reveal that the optimal method for minimizing performance disparities is to parallelize tasks within a fixed number of simultaneous evaluations, and that asymmetric population sizes can enhance efficiency, especially when computation times are skewed.

The recent discovery of HD 1660 is a direct imaging system comprising a star and a companion object located 1.07 arcseconds away, with the host star having a mass of 0.92 solar masses and a visual magnitude of 7.02. Based on the observed separation and the estimated 100 AU separation of the host star from the center of the galaxy, the object appears to be at a separation of 100-150 AU. A mass ratio of approximately 0.003 to 0.008 could indicate either a low-mass star or a planet, and the object's apparent visual magnitude is 14.8. However, the object's thermal emission was not detected by the JWST, with 3 sigma upper limits of 0.1 microKelvin for the 21 microKelvin, 0.1 microKelvin for the 36 microKelvin, and 0.1 microKelvin for the 56 microKelvin bands. These results suggest that the object's effective temperature is less than 300 K, and the object's mass is less than 0.008 solar masses. If the object's mass is less than 0.008 solar masses, the object's age must be at least 10 million years, and the object's albedo must be at least 0.5. If

The concept of an effective Floquet Hamiltonian, derived from the Floquet generator, has been proposed to describe periodically driven quantum systems. Initially, the Floquet generator's time-dependence complicates obtaining effective Floquet generators, making the search for its form a significant challenge. We successfully determined the effective time-independent Floquet generator, the Hamiltonian, for a specific type of periodic drive, the two-tone drive. In the process, the Floquet generator's expression is found to be divided into two distinct phases, with one phase being somewhat complicated and the other being very complex. Notably, the division into these two phases occurs when the Bessel function's argument equals a specific value. We also found that a specific type of phase-space transformation can greatly simplify the expression associated with one of these phases. We used our findings to establish a new effective generator for a periodic drive that repeats every two tones.

Our comprehensive examination of CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ across various Rh compositions reveals distinct magnetic characteristics. For $x \gtrsim 0.6$, the material exhibits magnetic behavior associated with long-range ordering. Magnetic data, as measured by DC and AC magnetization techniques, suggest a complex interplay of ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic ordering patterns. This intricate magnetic behavior persists even in the paramagnetic regime and is indicative of spin fluctuations. Heat capacity measurements show a significant reduction in the specific heat coefficient $\gamma$ with increasing $x$. This reduction suggests that spin fluctuations initially decrease and then potentially increase, which could be linked to the observed changes in the material's electronic structure, as revealed by resistivity and Hall coefficient measurements. These findings indicate that spin fluctuations may initially decrease and then increase with growing Rh content, potentially linked to a complex relationship between the material's carrier density and its specific heat coefficient $\gamma$.

Using the 100-m Radio Telescope, we examined the cold gas dynamics of a complex star-forming area, specifically the high-mass star-forming region G035.00-0.24, near the Galactic center. Our research focused on understanding the gas dynamics through observations of hydrogen gas and carbon monoxide. Our results revealed strong evidence for a hydrogen gas phenomenon known as HINSA in this region, and this is a highly sensitive indicator of a shock interaction between outflows and ambient gas. Our observations also showed significant cold hydrogen gas and carbon monoxide gas, located at various distances from the two young stars in the region. Our observations revealed a significant shock wave in region B, and this shock wave is likely caused by the outflow generated by the star G35.00-0.24B. Our research also suggests the presence of two dense gas filaments, located at the southern and northern sides of region A. Our observations indicate that region A is relatively stable, and this stability is likely due to the gas filaments.

We demonstrate the topological equivalence of all intermediate beta-transformations with a specific type of greedy beta-transformation that incorporates a hole at zero. Furthermore, we derive a method to calculate the largest hole size at zero that maintains homeomorphism for a given beta-transformation. This method is illustrated with concrete examples in base 3 and base phi, where $\phi$ represents the golden ratio.

The study presents a research analysis of $D^+ \to K^+ \mu^+ \mu^-$ and $D^+ \to \pi^+ \mu^+ \mu^-$ decays, focusing on an advanced region where qbar quarks are present and other relevant processes, such as $D^+ \to \pi^+ \pi^-\mu^+ \mu^+$, occur in the context of $LHCb$ data from $pp$ collisions at $7$ TeV. With $36.1$ femtoseconds of data recorded, this investigation aims to assess the impact of CP-violation and examine the potential new physics influences through measurement of S and P wave amplitudes.

It is widely acknowledged that deep neural networks excel at extracting features from a given dataset but struggle to apply this ability to datasets with different underlying characteristics. We propose a novel method called Adversarial Feature Extraction (AFE) that incorporates features into a classification model, which can handle diverse datasets. This approach involves two components: (1) a feature extractor that uses an adversarial process to detach it from dataset-specific characteristics, and (2) a supervised classifier that utilizes the features. Our approach was tested on six large-scale image datasets, and we found that AFE significantly outperformed existing methods, demonstrating improved generalization on out-of-distribution data.

In finite fields, we consider the plane $\mathbb{F}_q^2$ and the properties of arcs within it. A set of points $A$ is considered an arc if no three of its points are collinear. The objective of this paper is to count the occurrences of $k$-dimensional affine subspaces $\mathbb{F}_q^2$ that intersect with an $(q-k)$-arc $P$ in a specific manner, given the constraint that each of these subspaces passes through at most a certain number of points of $P$. The derived bounds have implications for the study of $k$-rarity and a conjecture proposed by S. Ball and J. Lambert concerning the existence of certain affine subspaces within arcs. Furthermore, these bounds provide a means to demonstrate the existence of $k$-rare arcs.

A pictorial proof shows that there are $\binom{n+2}{4}$ equilateral triangles in a regular $n$-sided triangle, with this also providing an alternative proof for the $\binom{r+1}{4}$ sum of squares formula.

Insights into Graph Neural Network (GNN) predictions are essential for improving their accuracy, reducing errors, and enhancing trust. However, existing methods for explaining these predictions are often inaccurate, computationally expensive, or based on static graphs. To address these limitations, we have developed a new approach called Temporal Counterfactual Explanation (Temporal CEX), which utilizes a temporal graph neural network and the IF-GNN framework to generate causal explanations for GNN predictions in temporal data. Through our approach, users can provide prior knowledge, such as GNN architecture and loss function, to obtain meaningful, causal, and spatial/temporal localized explanations. Experimental results have demonstrated that CEX effectively reduces computational costs, highlights the most significant graph nodes, and successfully identifies user-specified nodes as explanations.

The peculiar galaxy system RXCJ0232.2-4423 has been the subject of debate due to potential interactions between its two members, RXCJ0232.2-4420 and RXCJ0232.2-4423. In this study, researchers examined archival data and conducted a deep examination of RXCJ0232.2-4420, the more complex system. They discovered that RXCJ0232.2-4420 consists of two interacting systems, IC0232-1 and IC0232-2, which exhibit a temperature difference and have distinct morphologies. In contrast to expectations, RXCJ0232.2-4420 displays a core that is hotter than its outer regions, indicating the presence of an X-ray point source within IC0232-1. Researchers detected 21 molecular gas lines in RXCJ0232.2-4420, revealing a notable concentration of gas in IC0232-2. A gas-to-luminosity ratio was found to be significantly higher in RXCJ0232.2-4420 compared to other cool core systems. Moreover, researchers detected a gas outflow emanating from IC0232-2, which may be powered by activity in RXCJ02

A new unit type called the Legendre Memory Unit (LMU) has been developed for RNNs.
It's based on an information compression approach using a compact memory buffer,
which stores coefficients for a two-dimensional polynomial. As the input sequence
lengthens, the LMU's performance improves, outperforming similar RNNs in regression and classification tasks while using less parameters. In contrast to a transformer-based alternative, the LMU offers a significant speedup during both training and inference, approximately 10-50 times faster, according to experiments conducted on a range of datasets.

The concept of particles that interact weakly is integral to explaining dark matter, fundamental particles, and potentially the inflationary epoch.  In traditional particle physics, such particles are confined to high-energy interactions, but with significant advances in theoretical and numerical physics, low-energy processes can now be explored, albeit with complexities introduced by mediating degrees of freedom.  A new technique called Lepton Flavour Ejection is proposed to describe the feebly interacting particle's (FIP) low-energy interactions.  The method is illustrated by modeling axion-like particles' interactions with nucleons, facilitated by E-jecton, a theoretical framework that derives Lepton Flavour Ejection operators from their mediators, specifically the axion.  By employing an approximation that neglects the ejection of the axion, a comprehensive set of Lepton Flavour Ejection operators is generated and expressed in terms of properties like mass, decay constant, and conformal symmetry.  The resulting Lepton Flavour Ejection Lagrangian is then used to examine various interactions between axions and nucleons, particularly axion-induced electron-nucleon scattering, an emerging area of research proposed as a means to detect axion-like particles.

Language is a vital aspect of human existence, and its evolution is a complex phenomenon influenced by various factors, including the movement of people and interactions between them. This study aims to explore and model this process using a computational approach, which enables the examination of language dynamics on a large scale, taking into account real-world geographical features and the movement of individuals. Our model reveals that migration can lead to a significant impact on language distribution, with individuals often adopting a second language due to interactions with non-native speakers. Furthermore, our results suggest that a level of connectivity that is too high or too low can result in a uniform distribution of languages, with an optimal level of connectivity promoting a diverse language landscape. Our simulations also reveal that the long-term stability of a language depends on the balance between connectivity and population size, with larger populations being more likely to retain a language in the long term. Our research also indicates that the short-term dynamics of language adoption can have a lasting impact on the long-term language landscape, with rapid early adoption leading to more diverse language distributions. Overall, our findings contribute to our understanding of the complex interplay between migration and language adoption, and may have implications for the preservation of linguistic diversity in an increasingly globalized world.

PINNs have gained popularity for solving high-dimensional partial differential equations but their effectiveness is limited by a lack of theoretical understanding of their ability to learn complex functions. Existing research has shown that neural networks can approximate PDE solutions but their ability to learn solutions in a sequential manner has not been addressed. This work demonstrates that in order for neural networks to learn solutions to high-frequency PDEs, they must have enough parameters to accommodate the oscillations, and that adding more layers instead of adding more nodes in each layer allows for sequential learning of solutions. This is demonstrated by showing that adding layers enables networks to learn solutions to PDEs with increasingly complex patterns, and that this has implications for solving PDEs on large scales and at different scales.

We examine a two-wave system in the interval (-1,1), where one wave lacks damping and the other experiences partial Kelvin-Voigt damping. By employing transposition methods and ensuring conditions for internal localization of resolving operators, our research demonstrates the stability of this system under strong coupling. Notably, this is a first instance of exponential stability within a wave system that features no viscous damping. Furthermore, this work builds upon previous studies, showing that a similar system with viscous damping achieves exponential stability (see Theorem A). In contrast, when the damping mechanism changes to friction, resulting in a mixed wave-elastic system, stability shifts to polynomial decay under similar circumstances (see Theorem B).

To tackle the limitations of deep reinforcement learning, we've developed a new approach. Traditional deep reinforcement learning methods face two major limitations: the inability to gather enough data efficiently and issues with overfitting when using certain models. To overcome these problems, we combined deep reinforcement learning with generative adversarial games. This innovative approach allowed us to utilize generated data to improve the reinforcement learning process and mitigate overfitting caused by modeling issues. We established a framework for adversative learning to balance the modeling of state transitions and the reinforcement learning process. Our approach, known as adversative learning, demonstrated better results than its counterpart methods, particularly when dealing with limited data availability and overfitting issues.

We've developed a comprehensive theory for achieving optical nonreciprocity in any mode of a resonator by leveraging quantum effects. Our findings reveal that any change in a resonator's self-oscillating field's quantum properties can result in different effective nonlinear refractive indices when measured in opposite directions. This asymmetry in refractive index creates a reciprocal phase shift, ultimately producing optical nonreciprocity. Notably, achieving nonreciprocity doesn't necessitate the use of time-varying parameters or structures, as previously believed. Instead, self-sustained oscillations are sufficient to induce optical nonreciprocity. This theoretical framework provides new avenues for developing more efficient and versatile non-reciprocal optical devices.

We investigate the relationship between kernel functions and their corresponding
kernel gradients, specifically focusing on how these gradients serve as an
approximation of one another around a given point in an optimization landscape.
By examining the behavior of the kernel gradient in relation to the kernel, we
establish a criterion for accurately predicting the kernel's local maxima without
relying solely on the kernel itself. This condition is demonstrated to be both
necessary and sufficient for its predictability. Our analysis is further
extended to the context of non-convex kernel functions, revealing that the kernel
gradient can be used to construct a sequence of descent steps that efficiently
converge towards a local maximum in a bounded region within a polynomial number
of iterations. By utilizing a kernel with a Lipschitz continuous gradient, we
are able to develop more accelerated methods for finding local maxima in these
optimization landscapes. Our findings also have implications for the k-means
optimization problem, specifically that the optimization problem becomes more
tractable when a concave kernel function is employed.

A new type of detector, specifically a thin, low-heat capacity sensor made of lithium molybdate, has been utilized by the CRESST experiment to thoroughly examine dark matter. The ability of these detectors to accurately measure the energy released and the associated heat has enabled a detailed examination of potential dark matter particles in multiple areas, including dark photons, scalar particles with various interaction characteristics, and gravitons. This note will outline how the data collected by CRESST-III has been used to provide a comprehensive investigation of the mentioned dark matter candidates, including some that have not been thoroughly explored before, with the ultimate goal of laying a foundation for further research conducted by CRESST-VI.

Blind image deblurring is an ill-posed problem, necessitating the use of restrictive kernels to ensure a feasible solution and suppress unwanted outcomes. This research introduces a novel approach, Blind Image Deblurring via Kernel Mixture Structure Search, to tackle this challenge. By assuming a kernel mixture representation for the degradation kernel, our search strategy utilizes paired blurred and reference patches to obtain high-quality, reference-free blurred patches through weak enhancement. Subsequently, our k-meание algorithm enhances both the numerical robustness and numerical stability of the method. Comprehensive experiments on various datasets demonstrate the superiority of our method, particularly in the absence of reference images.

This paper introduces a concept of BiHom-Yang-Baxter pair on the double curved Rota-Baxter system, demonstrating how it influences the system and in turn, the Rota-Baxter system itself, with the system being equivalent to the BiHom-Yang-Baxter pair under certain conditions. Furthermore, we establish the existence of the Tensor product of curved BiHom-Yang-Baxter pairs, and ultimately show how a BiHom-Yang-Baxter element emerges from the Tensor product of curved Rota-Baxter elements.

Formal verification methods, like Hoare logic, aid programmers in creating error-free software, but applying them to complex tasks like autonomous driving is onerous due to the extensive formal specifications required. To address this challenge, we introduce formal goals - straightforward conditions that can be interpreted by both humans and machines. We have developed a framework that enables informal reasoning about the relationships between Hoare triples and formal goals using deductive goal frameworks. This innovation allows us to simplify reasoning about systems' properties as they reach target states and about the properties of individual commands. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to apply this approach to verify autonomous driving functionalities in a self-driving controller, bringing the formalized methods to new heights of practicality.

Distributed consensus is crucial for various distributed systems, such as distributed databases and blockchains, primarily due to their ability to synchronize data and ensure consistency. The Canopus distributed consensus protocol is a scalable and efficient solution that enables time-sensitive operations within a time frame. However, the system faces challenges related to the timing aspects of message transmission and the exponential increase in time slots due to varying node degrees. To address these issues, the system employs the earliest available message method, the first visit to neighbor (FVN) strategy, and the random early function (REF) strategy, which collectively minimize late messages, reduce the number of time slots, and lower communication overhead. The effectiveness of these strategies is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and numerical simulations, showing that they scale linearly with the number of nodes and significantly reduce the number of late messages and the required time slots.

The presence of cholesterol in cell membranes significantly affects their elasticity and rigidity. To comprehend this phenomenon, researchers have been investigating the impact of cholesterol on the membrane's bending properties. Using advanced computer simulations, researchers found that introducing cholesterol to lipid bilayers increases their bending modulus by 50 percent, thereby influencing the membranes' ability to form ruffles and vesicles. Notably, this change occurs without altering the inherent properties of the lipid bilayers, thereby offering valuable insights into the crucial role of cell membranes in biological processes.

This paper examines the loop quantum cosmological model for a Friedmann-Robertson-Walker universe with spatial curvature, as well as a homogeneous quadratic correction term. We analyze how the gravity of the universe and the cosmic fluid's gravity compete with each other, especially in relation to a critical matter density that marks the onset of quantum gravity effects. Our investigation reveals that the gravity of the universe will prevent these effects from arising when the correction term is significant enough, effectively preventing a big-bang or big-bounce scenario. Furthermore, we demonstrate that when the correction term dominates, the universe behaves like it has no beginning, with a big-bounce event occurring when the total energy density reaches a maximum value approximately equal to the Planck density.

The Pierre Auger Observatory catalog details 100 cosmic ray events logged between 2004 and 2020, associated with energies above 30 EeV, representing the highest recorded for this timeframe. The analysis encompasses both all-sky and targeted particle and extensive air-shower data, including a comprehensive map of cosmic ray sources, based on the recorded energies and arrival times, spanning nearly two decades.

Deep neural networks have become a popular choice for complex robotic tasks due to their ability to learn non-linear output mappings. However, their utility is limited by the lack of output probability distributions, resulting in unreliable predictions. This issue can be addressed by using deep probabilistic neural networks, which provide uncertainty estimates through stochastic sampling. A major obstacle in developing these models is the difficulty of incorporating uncertainty into deep nonlinear settings, particularly when working with variational autoencoders. This challenge is further compounded by the non-convex nature of the problem, leading to a significant gap between theoretical and practical implementations of deep probabilistic neural networks. Recent breakthroughs in stochastic variational autoencoders, employing Monte Carlo gradient estimation, have significantly improved the reliability of stochastic sampling, marking a major milestone in the field of deep probabilistic neural networks.

This paper examines the challenges associated with predicting traffic conditions using spatiotemporal information. Current models that rely on these predictions struggle with incorporating the spatial correlations within the test data, which compromises the accuracy of the forecast. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel approach that involves dividing the test data into smaller, spatially restricted sections and applying a traffic prediction model to each patch. By combining the predictions from overlapping patches, we achieve a more accurate forecast. Additionally, we introduce a mechanism to weight patch predictions based on their proximity to one another. Our approach yields significant performance gains, with a 1.5% improvement in model accuracy compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

This work demonstrates that Gray categories are precisely the triple categories, which implies that they are also tricategories without identity, establishing that strict Gray categories are equivalent to strict tricategories, rectifies a previous misunderstanding in literature and introduces the concept of pseudowritten categories, showing that they fit within a broader framework of weak categories, effectively generalizing both Gray categories and written categories.

Accurate identification and quantification of hippocampus atrophy are crucial in detecting early signs of neuropsychiatric disorders, making hippocampus segmentation a key challenge in medical imaging. A proposed deep learning-based method utilizes the hierarchical structure of the hippocampus, combining segmentation tasks in reverse order, beginning with hippocampus shape and ending with tissue classification. This approach incorporates a novel loss function designed to improve the accuracy of the reverse-order segmentation tasks. To evaluate its performance, this approach was applied to Automatic Hippocampus Segmentation Challenge data, showcasing superior results when compared to competing deep learning-based approaches, showcasing potential applications in the study of hippocampus structure and its potential role in neuropsychiatric disorders.

We've developed an advanced version of the double-slit experiment by introducing entangled photons generated through Spontaneous Parametric Down-Conversion. Our innovation lies in the creation of complex traversal patterns in a multi-path interferometer, where entangled photons from three sources intersect without any two traveling along the same path. This phenomenon, analogous to particle interactions at interaction points, reinforces our understanding of how traversals can be defined at the quantum level.

Observations from a NASA probe revealed the presence of the inner proton radiation belt, formed through the long-term accumulation of phase-space by an process involving the '2 days resonance' between the belt's protons and space waves. This phenomenon occurs when the waves' periods match the movement of protons in space, facilitated by a process where the waves affect proton movement in space over time. The findings indicate that the '2 days resonance' contributes significantly to the formation of the inner radiation belt.

A network's expressivity is its capacity to learn specific tasks or data patterns, and this property has a significant impact on the maximum efficiency of deep neural networks. Recent theories suggest that in very deep neural networks, expressivity often becomes the limiting factor due to the extensive amount of information and parameters involved. This paper explores a particular class of neural networks, known as convolutional networks, that operate on data in the form of square matrices. It delves into how these parameters scale, demonstrates that their expressivity is not a major limitation, and suggests that other factors, such as computational limitations, may be more influential in determining their capacity to learn. Additionally, the paper investigates how these networks can be adapted to various input dimensions and scales, showing that their expressivity is comparable across different configurations.

The problem of low-rank matrix completion in a federated learning setting, involving a central server and multiple participants, is investigated. A central server initially distributes randomly generated vectors, and each user collects data on their local machine. Then, they send a form of randomized response to the central server, which iteratively updates the form of these randomly distributed vectors. This process, which occurs over Z iterations, forms the basis of a new algorithm for matrix completion. This algorithm, which is called RML-Matrix-Z, is then applied to the low-rank matrix completion problem. It is found that RML-Matrix-Z, which is a form of distributed learning, is able to achieve the same level of accuracy as the best possible estimate that could be achieved if the data were not private. This is shown to be the case under the assumption that the data follows a sub-Gaussian distribution. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that RML-Matrix-Z, which is a form of distributed learning, can be adapted to work with other forms of data distribution. This is done by using a form of iterative reweighting, which allows the algorithm to converge to a form of accurate estimate that could be achieved if the data were not private. This is shown to be the case under the assumption that the data has bounded support. Finally, it is demonstrated that RML-Matrix-Z, which is a form of distributed learning, can be used in practice, with a level of accuracy that is comparable to the best

Polycyclic Aromatic Molecules, specifically interstellar in origin, have been extensively studied for several decades, contributing to our understanding of interstellar dust since the 1970s. Advances in technology allow us to detect and analyze these complex hydrocarbons in greater detail, particularly with the recent addition of space-based instruments capable of observing them in specific wavelength ranges. A notable study published in 2021 exemplifies this enhanced detection capability through a comprehensive analysis of PAHs in a stellar environment.

Research into planet formation around low-mass stars has been lacking,
particularly in the area of understanding how it occurs in the dense
cluster environment where NGC 188 is located. A thorough examination of
data from the Spitzer Infrared Spectrograph revealed a comprehensive
inventory of molecules in the circumstellar disk surrounding the star HD 64760,
a very low-mass star. Moreover, further observations in the same cluster
have shown that only one other star, HD 64760's neighbor, displays a disk
signature. Consequently, a more in-depth analysis of the cluster's
demographics, considering the low-mass star population, led to the
conclusion that the density of disks around such stars is relatively low.
This finding is in line with theories of planet formation, particularly
those that suggest the process is impeded by gravitational instability and
turbulence. Furthermore, the study of the density of low-mass stars in the
cluster led to the estimation of the minimum mass of such objects,
approximately 18-55 Jupiter masses. As a result, the study's implications
for the process of planet formation, particularly in the context of the
gravitational instability theory, have been discussed.

Consider a graph where every vertex can be either off or on. Define a function $\rho$ on $V$ as a configuration of lights. In an interactive game, two players take turns. Player A chooses a vertex $v$ and flips its state, and then player B chooses a neighbor of $v$, say $u$, and flips its state as well. This process is repeated until the game ends. Initial configuration of lights is chosen by A, and if the game can end in an all-dark state, then it is called $\G$-cleavable.
