This research contributes to the understanding of the historical development of worldwide seasonal fire patterns over the past 50 years by utilizing data from the ECJFED database to backtrack the past of global annual fire days for days with confirmed active fires. We discovered that the majority of global regions have experienced maximum fire seasons not exceeding 9 months, accounting for approximately 88% of observations. Conversely, shorter fire seasons of less than 4 months are relatively rare, occurring in only 10% of observations. We also observed significant disparities in the duration of fire seasons across different latitudes, altitudes, and climate zones. Moreover, we observed substantial variations in the number of fire days from year to year, indicating high interannual variability. Our findings underscore the significance of conducting further studies on the historical development of seasonal fire patterns in conjunction with past climate changes.

This research focuses on the variation of six distinct metrics for evaluating the morphological intricacy of languages, previously proposed by Bertinetto et al. The investigation centers on two key areas of inquiry: Firstly, the statistical correlations of these metrics were examined and found to yield remarkable outcomes, with the first principal component to notably explain 80% of the variance in the dataset. The remaining variance is attributed to the secondary component, contributing 13% of the total variance and primarily representing the distinction between languages exhibiting low morphological complexity and agglutinative languages such as Turkish and Zulu. The remaining component accounts for approximately 7% of the total variance. The study further reveals the remarkable consistency of these metrics across various typological frameworks, with the former's estimates closely aligning with estimates made by the latter using a comparable set of languages.

The second area of the investigation involved a correlation analysis to determine whether the complexity of a language's morphology correlates with its age in a family's language tree. The results indicate that a language family's initial language typically displays the lowest level of morphological complexity and that, over time, a language family tends to become more complex in its morphology.

We investigated subhaloes within the A1689 gravitational lens, a system examined through standard cold dark matter and self-interacting dark matter models. We calculated the probability distribution of self-interacting dark matter subhaloes, and found it to be consistent with observations made of standard cold dark matter. Furthermore, we discovered through simulations that spherical, isolated subhaloes exhibit mass loss, and developed a model to describe this phenomenon, which is then used to analyze properties of clumps within the A1689 system. We found the model to be in agreement with measured mass and size ratios, and made predictions for observed surface brightness ratios resulting from mass loss. We also found that self-interacting dark matter standard deviations are greater than cold dark matter predictions, and demonstrated through simulations and actual observations that this can lead to distinguishing between the two models.

This research focuses on reducing the complexity of parametric partial differential equations (PPDEs) by finding an accurate approximation space for the solutions of the equations. Given incomplete information, this research uses two primary sources: initial conditions and partial observations of the solutions. Based on incomplete data describing solution snapshots, this research constructs a preliminary low-dimensional approximation subspace. This process is refined using two-dimensional spaces that are further enriched through partial observations, resulting in a more accurate and reliable approximation subspace.

This study introduces the m-arcsinh Kernel Mean Feature Extraction (m-ar-K-FastICA) method, an enhanced approach for extracting features from data with varying levels of randomness. Unlike previous methods, m-ar-K-FastICA utilizes an innovative estimator that is unaffected by data outliers and efficiently manages random data. In both artificial and real-world image datasets, our findings indicate that m-ar-K-FastICA consistently outperforms the kernel ICA method based on the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion, with improved performance becoming more pronounced as the size of the dataset increases. Furthermore, the proposed method surpasses the kernel FastICA results in terms of m-H-s-I-C-A/FastICA p-values, exhibiting a significant difference of 0.001 for the MNIST dataset.

Identifying patterns within data streams from social media platforms such as Twitter is an emerging challenge in data mining. Due to the immense volume of data, it's impractical to store all of it. Instead, the existing data is utilized to monitor events like disasters, political trends, and more. Our paper introduces an algorithm capable of detecting such patterns from social media data, specifically for the identification of disaster occurrences on Twitter.

We establish the optimal Lipschitz regularity of very weak solutions for a specific class of isotropic second-order elliptic PDEs with random coefficients, characterized by the form $\sum_{j, k=1}^d a_{j k}(x) \partial_j \partial_k u = f$. By employing a novel approach, we derive and prove regularity estimates of the form $\|u\|_{W^{1, \infty}} \lesssim \|f\|_{BMO^{-1}}$ through localized testing argument techniques from stochastic homogenization. This method is then adapted to establish the sharp regularity of solutions for deterministic elliptic systems and systems with mixed boundary conditions.

The presence of a large number of stable compounds in the cobalt-rich area presents challenges for the development of accurate phase diagrams, necessitating the use of approximations due to the unfeasibility of experimental verification for many substances. To overcome these limitations, extensive first-principles calculations involving 109 cobalt-rich compounds were conducted, aiming to identify the most stable phases and their corresponding local maxima in the energy landscape. To address the challenge of temperature effects, the quasi-harmonic approximation was applied to the identified stable cobalt-rich compounds to estimate their Gibbs free energy values at temperatures of 300K, 600K, and 900K. To facilitate the creation of the phase diagrams, free energy differences between the stable phases and all considered subphases were determined. Furthermore, the calculated results were benchmarked against the available experimental and first-principles findings in the existing literature.

In the field of display advertising, real-time bidding has emerged as a key strategy for ad trading, enabling instant decisions to be made on whether to bid and at what price while processing each impression. This study focuses on making optimal bidding choices under uncertain conditions, taking into account factors such as click-through rates, conversion rates, and individual risk preferences. To achieve this, we developed a comprehensive framework grounded in Markov decision processes, which allows for an in-depth analysis of the impact of different risk preferences on in-session advertising outcomes. Through risk-sensitive utility functions, we examined the effects of risk preferences on utility and unit price bids, revealing unique features of each approach. Furthermore, we investigated how different risk preferences influence optimal unit price bids over time, identifying specific patterns such as decreasing or unimodal curves. To validate our findings, we conducted simulations using data from a leading US company providing real-time decision-making interfaces, which confirmed our theoretical predictions.

Non-classical properties of quantum systems are crucial in quantum information processing. We've established that the creation of a specific property called Wigner negativity between two parties is possible if and only if the state they share allows for quantum steering. This important finding has significant implications as it provides a clear method for verifying quantum steering. The validity of our argument is further confirmed by demonstrating the ability of quantum systems to create Wigner negativity in a specific two-party scenario, which in turn makes the creation of non-classical resources possible using experimentally feasible methods.

Accurate secure boundary analysis is crucial for practical quantum key distribution, yet the impact of random seed uniformity on the secure key rate remains unexplored. To address this, we developed a method for evaluating the seed uniformity that can be applied to the BB84 protocol. Our findings indicate that even minor variations in the seeds can significantly lower the system's output secure key rate. Furthermore, we implemented the BB84 scheme on a Zynq-7000 FPGA, demonstrating the necessity of high-quality random seeds for achieving the theoretical secure boundary.

This research paper confirms that specific types of Bertrand curves found in higher-dimensional space can actually occur and exist in their current form. In contrast to previous studies, this finding challenges the notion that one such curve type is impossible or non-existent. By working in a complex Euclidean space with an even number of dimensions, the authors derive the parametrization for a general timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve. This involves establishing key relationships between various curve properties and identifying essential conditions for the existence of Bertrand curves. The study also reveals that the parametrization for the existing timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curves can be achieved through a combination of linear functions, an exponential expression, and the lightlike (1,3)-helix case.

We establish a theorem on the convergence in total variation of Feller's diffusion, which describes a continuous, non-negative population, with a broader scope than the existing results, and without relying on the condition of uniformization. The novel proof utilizes a diffusion approximation of a birth-death process, contrasting the Feller diffusion with a birth-death process having a dynamically changing capacity, which may vary continuously, and ensures an upper bound on the dynamic capacity.

In this research, we introduce a theoretical method utilizing effective vertex functions within waveguide QED systems to address multi-photon scattering issues involving multiple channels. Our approach allows us to compute multi-photon scattering amplitudes without directly referencing the time evolution process. We apply this method to solve complex multi-photon scattering problems involving non-interacting waveguide networks featuring multiple channels. Furthermore, we extend its application to systems connected to waves and demonstrate its effectiveness through a study of the Knill-Laflamme-Wootters protocol in a triple system scenario. Additionally, we apply our method to tackle the multi-photon clock problem in systems featuring photon delay lines.

A potential way to study low-mass dark matter is by utilizing boosted dark matter interactions. The framework of dark matter interactions with an enhanced momentum transfer is described using structure factors, which can be constrained by data. Our analysis of proton structure factors reveals that, for boosted dark matter, the scattering process is predominantly independent of time. Furthermore, we use the findings from QCD and gravitational studies of nucleons to predict proton recoil energy spectra in enhanced momentum transfer scenarios.
This note employs Faulhaber's Formula to elucidate why odd Bernoulli numbers equate to zero.

Continuous phase modulation (CPM) signals offer superior power efficiency to other linear modulation methods, and their complexity can be further reduced by eliminating a carrier phase recovery scheme. Non-coherent differential detection, the most basic form of CPM, suffers from severely limited bandwidth due to its sensitivity to phase noise. Researchers have attempted to increase its bandwidth, yet their methods have been limited by the necessity for memory-intensive operations. This paper proposes a new receiver design that effectively expands the bandwidth of conventional differential detection, with minimal additional computational burden. The method's optimality is mathematically justified for any CPM signal. The proposed system is evaluated in terms of its performance and complexity.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback, typically gathered through surveys ranking or scoring generated outputs. However, such approaches often rely on coarse-grained metrics, which may not adequately reflect the nuanced preferences of humans. This paper proposes an alternative method that allows humans to directly edit suboptimal text, which implicitly yields preference pairs for training reward models. Notably, this human editing can be viewed as a form of instruction-following, leading to the development of RRL, a novel framework that simultaneously learns a reward model and generates edits. In experiments, the framework outperformed existing approaches in multiple evaluation scenarios.

We outline an approach to extract nucleon structure functions from lattice QCD calculations using semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering processes. This method can also help isolate the Generalized Parton Distributions (GPDs) at GPD pole Q^2 values through finite temperature lattice QCD calculations. To understand GPs, spin-dependent structure functions $g_1$ and $g_2$ are crucial. By measuring $g_1$ and $g_2$ on the lattice with high precision, we can determine nucleon's spin structure and its contribution. To achieve this goal, the J-PARC E155B experiment has set standards for measuring $g_1$ and $g_2$ in experiments. Our approach involves projecting nucleon's GPDs from the GPD pole to the deep virtual Compton scattering (DVCS) limit and relating it to inclusive structure functions $F_1$, $F_2$, $g_1$, and $g_2$. By incorporating additional information from transverse kinematic variables, we can distinguish between $F_1$ and $F_2$ as well as $g_1$ and $g_2$. This technique relies on the Altarelli-Parisi evolution equations and enables the extension of GPD extractions from the GPD pole to the DVCS limit.

In recent years, topological codes have been extensively researched, particularly the surface code which drives quantum computing applications, although the codes with lower density error thresholds are often overlooked. This study explores a theoretical model of a dynamic, frustrated Toric code that isn't at equilibrium and exhibits a tunable phase transition from a codes phase to a synaptic phase, which doesn't have a code property. This new model, dubbed the adjustable Toric code, is proposed as a foundational framework for developing a more efficient, dense topological code that can support synapses, essential for processing information and driving learning capabilities, potentially enabling the development of bio-inspired quantum computers.

We investigate the eigenspectra of large, randomly perturbed, symmetric matrices whose entries are independent and identically distributed. As the matrix size $N$ approaches infinity, the limiting distribution of complex eigenvalues' imaginary parts no longer aligns with the $2$-dimensional Gaussian distribution, under the assumption that the variance of the matrix entries grows faster than $1/\sqrt{N}$.

Our approach relies on a novel local law derived from a generalization of a prior result established by Erdős, Yau, and Yu for random band matrices, where the parameter $K$ scales polynomially with $N$. This local law demonstrates the validity of a modified semicircle law for specific regimes of $K$.

The key achievement of this work lies in its correlation to linearization methods, where the problem can be reduced to analyzing certain polynomial equations of increasing degree based on the value of $K$.

Ultimately, we derive a precise asymptotic expression for the limiting density of complex eigenvalues in terms of an integral over a quadratic polynomial, whose coefficients are derived from Chebyshev polynomials, effectively providing an analytical solution to this problem for specific regimes where the variance of the matrix entries grows faster than $1/\sqrt{N}$.

Recent advancements in dialogue systems have been attributed to using end-to-end transformer models, but these models struggle with understanding the underlying dialogue context and often lack robustness, especially when dealing with out-of-domain data. A novel solution presented in this research involves using Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) to describe the underlying semantic framework of dialogue, enabling training a decoder model that predicts the progression of dialogue context. A significant dataset has been created, consisting of 50,000 annotated dialogue transcripts, to facilitate the training of robust and out-of-box dialogue decoding models. Experimental evaluations on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that employing AMR-based auxiliary learning leads to enhanced dialogue modeling capabilities.

To establish a universal standard for algorithmic interpretability, we need a measurement framework that's universally accepted. An ideal framework would be precise, versatile, adaptable to changes, and easy to grasp for those outside the field, while also addressing various forms of interpretability. We establish a measurement standard for algorithmic interpretability that captures its nuanced meanings and responds positively to increased transparency. Additionally, our framework aids in dissecting the algorithmic decision-making process of Gradient Boosted Decision Trees.

Anomaly detection without labeled data is a pressing issue, especially when dealing with complex, high-dimensional data. This study presents a new method called weBCA that harnesses the power of weak supervision in anomaly detection. By utilizing unsupervised image segmentation to create weak labels, we employ these to train a supervised autoencoder that identifies patterns typical of normal images. As a result, the hidden representations learned in these normal patterns serve as a baseline, enabling the detection of anomalies based on their deviation from this baseline. This method allows the use of domain-specific knowledge to guide weak label generation, enhancing the sensitivity of anomaly detection. This is demonstrated through the use of weBCA in analyzing retinal microaneurysms in retinal fundus images and achieving improved detection accuracy compared to unsupervised methods. Moreover, weBCA is found to perform competitively with other supervised anomaly detection methods that rely on synthetic training data.

A novel approach for modelling extreme values across various time series is presented. This method employs maximum likelihood estimation using a combination of fixed and random effects, with some parameters designed to remain consistent regardless of the threshold chosen for analysis. This allows for accurate predictions of extreme events at unknown future thresholds without the need for re-estimating model parameters. This method is demonstrated using simulated data and real-world examples of UK temperature and Australian rainfall extremes, which highlight the method's ability to enhance prediction accuracy at future, unknown thresholds.

This analysis explores the intersection area of a specific shape when cut through at different angles. Given that the shape's cross-section at any point in space is symmetrical, the average cross-sectional area is determined. The objective is to identify the conditions under which the average cross-sectional area reaches its maximum value.

This research paper introduces a new dataset called COMPOZITE, which enables a 
variety of natural language understanding tasks, including composition tasks in 
commonsense knowledge graphs. Specifically, it targets inductive reasoning tasks 
where multiple hypotheses must be evaluated against a given premise using 
inferred relationships from the knowledge graph. Furthermore, the proposed 
dataset includes a range of additional tasks such as open-ended story 
completion, paraphrase generation, and inductive task-related question answering, 
all of which are facilitated by a new COMPOZITE graph. The paper outlines these 
various associated tasks and examines their connections to one another.

A key goal of the Hi-GAL survey carried out by the Herschel satellite, aimed at mapping the Galactic plane's warm dust and emission from the HEAT survey, has an ambitious goal of studying star formation across the entire Milky Way. Utilizing three high-resolution filters, the survey covers an extensive area of 200 square degrees, spanning from $\ell$ = 0 to 200, in three frequency bands: 49.2, 140, and 258 $\mu$m, with 35" resolution. The data's quality is assessed using simulations based on the Hi-GAL pipeline processing. The simulations evaluate the survey's completeness and accuracy in recovering dust temperature, surface brightness, and HEAT dust clump properties. The results reveal that for HEAT clumps with an F$_{49.2\mu m}$ flux above 10 Jy, dust clump masses are recovered with 80% accuracy, but this drops below 60% for fainter sources. On the other hand, for massive clumps, F$_{140\mu m}$ fluxes are recovered with 80% accuracy, but this source population is incomplete, missing approximately 50% of the total number of clumps. In addition, F$_{258\mu m}$ fluxes are recovered with 80% accuracy for the most luminous clumps, but this is only

Our investigation of the first-generation stars in 14 globular clusters reveals 
new findings regarding their peculiar metallicities, particularly in relation to 
element composition variations. Utilizing data from the Gaia-DR2 chromosome maps, 
we established that iron-poor star populations can also exhibit super-metalic 
abundances, in addition to the commonly observed sub-metalic ones. Interestingly, 
these star populations display a preference towards the outer regions of the 
globular clusters, although iron content correlations with radial distribution 
vary among the examined clusters. Furthermore, iron ratios do not correlate 
directly with the globular clusters' metallicity or age, implying a complexity 
underlying the formation processes of the star populations in question.

To facilitate a deeper understanding of single file systems, we develop a generalised Riesz derivative model that effectively captures their collective and anomalous characteristics. We derive an asymptotic solution to this model, which includes a comprehensive description of the density profile near boundaries under various conditions. This allows for single file behaviour to emerge even when the derivative exponent is non-integer and sub-critical (<2). The proposed solution is validated through comparison with results from Riesz derivative exponent 2, which demonstrates its accuracy in sub-critical cases. Additionally, single file properties, including the mean waiting time, are found to scale anomalously and depend on the initial particle distribution.

Quantum mechanics' causal relationship is weakly expressed as an equality rather than a strict rule due to the presence of additional solutions. This is particularly true for quantum correlations that cannot be explained classically. Since classical causality can be defined through Bayes' rule, it is proposed that a bayesian framework can also be applied to quantum mechanics. However, this approach has a limitation: it cannot reduce to the standard formulation of quantum mechanics based on amplitudes, and it also fails to provide the standard, unambiguous prediction for measurement outcomes when sequential measurements are involved. While this quantum analogue of Bayes' rule is consistent with existing theories and experiments, it is likely to lead to new theoretical and practical developments.

We initially report findings regarding corrections to system size for the state equation, trace anomaly, and speed of sound, using three specific theoretical frameworks: the SU(2) and SU(3) Hamilton-Cached Hadron Resonance Models, and the SU(3) Quark-Meson Model. These results are based on fT values calculated in system volume. Additionally, we examine finite system volume corrections to the state equation, specifically for pressure and energy density, in the SU(3) Quark-Meson Model, and we discuss the impact of these corrections on the latter framework.

In a 1-dimensional relative prime formal group law context, specifically for Ext-groups related to Steenrod algebras, a crucial algebraic transfer homomorphism is investigated. For a particular prime number, p, a comprehensive algorithm is developed to compute the image of this homomorphism, and it is demonstrated that this image comprises all groups that are nontrivially generated.

Astronomers have limited access to far UV radiation from space due to its
high opacity in Earth's atmosphere. To overcome this limitation, the HAT-FUV
facility was designed to allow researchers to observe far UV radiation from
space using ground-based equipment. This facility incorporates a hydrogen
absorption cell capable of capturing far UV light and was designed to be
installed at the Cassegrain focus of telescopes, specifically the 2.05-meter
INSU/CNRS telescope at the La Silla Observatory in Chile. To assess the
facility's performance, researchers conducted a proof-of-concept experiment
using the INSU-CNRS telescope at a wavelength of 158.88 nm and found that the
detected hydrogen Lyman-alpha line had a resolution of 1.2 Angstroms and an
equivalent width of 0.02 Angstroms. This finding demonstrates the facility's
ability to detect atomic hydrogen in the far field, although further research
is required to improve its sensitivity and accuracy.

Optimal distributed feedback control strategies, designed to achieve consensus on a target value defined as the average of all agents' initial states, are proposed. The effectiveness of these strategies is demonstrated by their application to Graph Symmetric Systems, where the GSS property—characterized by systems with state symmetries and optimal symmetric solutions—is shown to be both necessary and sufficient for achieving this consensus. The development of these strategies relies on the application of Theorem 1, which is derived from modifications to results from [1], and which establishes that for systems with invariant states, it is possible to construct a feedback control law, dependent on current states, that ensures the system converges to those invariant states. The inclusion of a numerical example is intended to highlight the NSS property's limitations in multi-agent systems.

Image search algorithms that retrieve and identify copied images from vast databases comprise two main components: a neural network that translates an image into a semantic representation, and an advanced search technique. This work reviews the existing field of image copy search and examines the strengths and weaknesses of various neural networks and advanced algorithms. We then evaluate the performance of multiple image representations in conjunction with different hashing techniques and search methods. Our findings indicate that a nearest neighbor search is most suitable for short representations, while a beam search performs best for detailed representations. Furthermore, we discover that nearest neighbor measures such as the Euclidean distance yield superior accuracy compared to other measures like the Hamming distance or cosine similarity. Our research also highlights the potential benefits of incorporating copy search techniques from natural language processing, such as beam search and indexing with Jaccard similarity or Brown distance.

This study examines the possibility of authenticating information theoretically when using the physical layer in the presence of an adversary. Considering scenarios where the channel is either Gaussian or bounded by a certain peak signal, the researchers establish that a specific threshold of channel noise must be surpassed to allow for these types of authentication. When considering a more restrictive bounded channel and a specific coding strategy, the researchers found that a new threshold can be established. Interestingly, these thresholds are not affected by the intensity of the channel's adversarial interference. Furthermore, when these researchers placed no constraints on the channel's upper bounds, they discovered that the capacity to authenticate is contingent upon specific relationships between channel noise and adversarial interference, while also being able to tolerate a certain threshold of adversarial interference. Lastly, these researchers identified scenarios where a small, albeit non-zero, rate of authentication can be achieved, as well as scenarios where this rate is completely inconceivable.

Reevaluating the "random walk" and Brownian motion concepts in light of a 2012 study, we analyzed the dynamics of Brownian particles on a tilted random landscape under an applied constant force. When the bias force overcomes friction, these particles enter a running state and display superdiffusive motion and thermal plasma formation, even at low temperatures. When the bias force is insufficient, they exhibit a transitional phase characterized by a 50/50 distribution of walking and drifting motions. We derived an analytical expression for the probability distribution function of the particles in this transition zone, revealing the persistence of thermal plasma formation and superdiffusion under an applied constant force, driven by a dominant anomalous diffusion coefficient determined by specific system parameters.

This paper presents structured estimates of the fiscal multiplier in response to government spending surprises using a non-parametric approach, which only relies on the assumption that government spending is determined by its own history. The results suggest that during normal times, the initial multiplier for a shock that reduces economic activity reaches about 0.6 within three months, significantly lower than similar estimates for similar shocks in other studies. Conversely, during recessions, the initial multiplier for a shock that boosts economic activity reaches about 1.2 within three months, significantly higher than similar shocks in other studies. Furthermore, these effects persist at roughly half their initial levels for six months. Characteristics such as whether the economy is experiencing high inflation, whether the central bank has reached its inflation target, and whether the central bank has reached its zero lower bound on interest rates do not appear to have a significant impact on the magnitude of these effects.

We investigate the influence of the electromagnetic quantum vacuum on the angular momentum of a charge q moving in a uniform magnetic field. The orbital angular momentum generated is due to photons in the vacuum that emit an energy back to the charge in proportion to n^2, a greater increase than that of the -2n\hbar of a charge in a Landau orbit.

Research into Fine-grained Named Entity Typing (FET) has seen a significant boost in
performance thanks to advancements made in Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs).
However, the PLMs' performance is hindered by the challenges of representing multi-class data in Euclidean spaces.
Our research proposes a novel solution to this problem by leveraging hyperbolic space, the preferred framework for encoding hierarchical data.
We introduce Hyperbolic FET, a framework that employs the farthest point clustering algorithm to convert FET data into hyperbolic space, resulting in significant gains in performance.
Empirical evidence shows that our framework outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods on FET benchmarks, with the exception of the CoNLL 2003 dataset.
Additionally, the proposed framework's effectiveness is further demonstrated through its application to joint NER and Type tasks in the 2020 NLP system tasks at ACL NAACL.

This paper establishes upper limits on the Hankel determinants for the $H_2(3)(f)$ and $H_2(4)(f)$ special forms in univalent function theory, specifically for functions $f$ in the class $\mathcal{B}(\phi)$ with specific constraints on the analytic function $\phi$.

Achieving optimal performance from virtualized cloud data centers is complicated by the challenge of managing dynamic workloads and resource constraints. Virtual machines (VMs) migrate to balance loads and resource utilization, but do so reactively, which can lead to performance degradation during the process. Load balancing strategies can be categorized into two types: reactive migration and preemptive partitioning. Our research explores an innovative approach combining these strategies to optimize performance and reliability. The "Prepartition" method assigns weights to virtual machines and procures services proactively when their resources become insufficient. By doing so, it minimizes service unavailability and maximizes applications' QoS. The proposed "Prepartition" approach outperforms the traditional reactive migration by reducing resource underutilization by 10-15% and maintaining a similar Level of Service (LoS) with a lower weight.

In modeling interactions between competing entities, such as financial markets, researchers often rely on a game-theoretic framework where each agent seeks to maximize its own payoff, and stable outcomes are expected to be near a Nash equilibrium. However, in some cases, such as a zero-sum game between two agents with incomplete market information, the outcome does not meet a Nash equilibrium, posing a challenge to this type of model. This issue is illustrated in a two-player game that models the trading of a single asset with incomplete dynamics, and whose optimal strategies for both players are described by a coupled system of coupled-forward-backward stochastic differential equations. This system is shown to have a unique solution, which is used in a model of fair competition where both players have incomplete information.

This study tackles the issue of assessing causal influences in cases where some variables involved in ensuring causal validity are incompletely known. It develops an innovative assessment metric, referred to as the causal deficiency score, along with accompanying statistical measures. The causal deficiency score evaluates the extent to which observed data aligns with the causal validity criteria, while accompanying p-values and confidence intervals provide additional insights into the causal effect's reliability. Building upon a theoretical framework rooted in Bayesian analysis, this approach enables effective handling of incomplete information about the variables in question. A simulation study demonstrates the practical application and effectiveness of this proposed assessment method.

This paper introduces a groundbreaking system called DefenseNet, a distributed machine learning framework for enhancing the security of industrial control systems. ICS attacks have become increasingly severe, with the potential to cause significant damage. We propose a novel approach where a central sensor node can request assistance from a group of edge nodes to detect and prevent attacks. To achieve this, we employ a novel model where the edge nodes continuously update their machine learning models based on feedback from the central node. We analyze this framework's performance using theoretical metrics and compare our results to existing centralized and distributed systems. We validate our approach through simulations on a real power grid, showing that it can effectively detect various types of attacks.

A precise summary of a text requires both an in-depth understanding of different language nuances and a vast training dataset. While English text summarization models have been developed, they face challenges in achieving accuracy for other language formats due to the complexities of translating English data into other language formats, which can introduce inaccuracies. To overcome this, a novel approach called the Universal Summary Encoder (USE) has been designed to directly process text from other language formats without the need for translation. By employing a multi-layered structure, USE can learn a unified representation of the text, using it to both generate a summary and a corresponding knowledge representation. Furthermore, a model called the Neural Summarization Autoencoder (NSA) has been developed to learn a representation of the text and generate a summary simultaneously. The USE and NSA models have been successfully tested on the English summarization dataset Distant Summary Reading Graph, with both models achieving high accuracy rates of over 90%.

We establish the definition and certain attributes of S-rings of Krull type, in addition to examining the properties of such structures, particularly independent S-rings of type A. We establish that every infinite independent S-ring of type A contains a nontrivial principal ideal within a C-algebra of such independent S-rings, while also determining an isomorphism criterion for these rings based on their ideal structures.

Recent discoveries of isolated brown dwarfs with interstellar medium accretion suggest that brown dwarf and planetary objects can have free-floating counterparts in space. To identify potential accretion candidates, we conducted an in-depth study of two high-proper-motion stars, HIP 1481 and HIP 88399, using Archival data and new observations. This led to the detection of potential high-contrast near-infrared companions, estimated to be 10-100 Jupiter masses and 2-10 Jupiter masses, respectively. Further analysis confirmed these objects are likely real, and their spectral characteristics resemble those of brown dwarfs. This discovery makes HIP 1481 and HIP 88399 unique candidates for accretion, as they possess the necessary properties, including old age, low mass, and dense surrounding dust and gas. Upcoming facilities, such as the James Webb Space Telescope, will enable further investigation into these intriguing objects.

We introduce a novel approach called VAE4ECE, which utilizes a two-stage method to achieve superior reconstruction results for arbitrary shapes. The first stage involves employing a standard autoencoder to initially compress and reconstruct the input. The encoder produces a latent representation, and the decoder maps it back to the original space. In the second stage, we apply a variational autoencoder to refine the compressed latent space, leveraging adversarial training to generate a more natural representation. By combining these techniques, the proposed VAE4ECE achieves significant advantages, including improved reconstruction quality and faster convergence, as demonstrated through experiments on multiple datasets.

Smart home technology is rapidly gaining traction, yet concerns about its
vulnerability to cyber threats persist due to the limited protection offered
by traditional cybersecurity methods. This study explores the potential for
leveraging blockchain technology to enhance smart home security through a
private blockchain called HomeChain. By utilizing a private blockchain,
HomeChain offers enhanced security and performance over public blockchains
while still preserving user anonymity. A theoretical analysis demonstrates
HomeChain's suitability for smart home networks, featuring a functional
demonstrator that integrates with existing smart home systems through a user
friendly application called ChainHome. A comparative evaluation of public and
private blockchain implementations in a smart home network has shown HomeChain
to offer superior security, speed, and scalability.

A novel approach to quantizing log-likelihood ratio storage using deep learning is presented, which can significantly reduce the memory required for storing information. The method involves a two-part process: an encoder that generates a set of basis vectors and a binary representation for each vector, and an autoencoder that reconstructs the original LRLs from the binary data. The encoder and autoencoder are simultaneously optimized end-to-end, allowing the approach to adapt to non-Gaussian LRL distributions. When applied to a specific dataset from a large-scale spam database, this method achieved a 4.27x reduction in memory while maintaining a 99.99% accuracy.

We have devised three new algorithmic methods for analyzing the upward planarity of directed graphs that may contain cycles. First, we've created a linear-time algorithm to transform an acyclic graph into one that has no cycles and maintains its original upward planarity properties. This can be done efficiently in line with time complexity of O(m+n). Second, we developed a method to find an equivalent acyclic graph with minimal vertices and edges, achieving this in the same linear time. Third, for a graph that has cycles, we created an linear-time solution to identify a subset of vertices and edges whose removal would result in an upward planar acyclic graph. This solution has a time complexity of O(m+n).

The classification of crowdsourced, noisy image data presents a significant challenge due to its complexity. In particular, separating such data into categories based on content (scene images vs. object images) and difficulty (easy vs. hard images) is difficult due to the images' inherent challenges. In our research, a method is proposed to automatically categorize crowdsourced image data based on two categories (scene vs. object, and easy vs. hard) using two primary criteria: primary tag frequency distributions (for scene vs. object classification) and visual features (for hardness classification). We assess this approach through experiments on various object images (e.g., COCO, VisIP) and scene/hard images (e.g., IPIN, VisIP), demonstrating its general applicability and adaptability.

For semiflows with uniformly or nonuniformly expanding dynamics, which exhibit exponential decay in correlations, we can prove the exponential decay in the H\"older norm of the transfer operators acting on smooth observables.

A particular matrix known as a covering array has specific characteristics regarding the repeated occurrence of unique combinations in its submatrices. The size and characteristics of these matrices are constrained by a set of bounds, and researchers have been striving to determine the maximum or minimum dimensions of these matrices for given parameters. Recent advancements have focused on modifying these matrices using computer algorithms to achieve specific effects, such as reducing their size. This paper outlines a method for altering specific components of these modified matrices while maintaining their required characteristics, allowing a better understanding of their construction and potential improvements.

This paper examines a class of nonlocal games, specifically where the players' winning probabilities are limited by a specific inequality known as the Inequality of Tsirelson. We investigate how these probabilities change in response to noise affecting the shared entangled state, finding that noisy versions of maximally entangled states are particularly susceptible to noise. We derive a precise formula for how this noise is quantified and use it to calculate how the bound changes in response to noise, specifically demonstrating that this bound changes in a non-smooth manner. Additionally, we provide an accurate estimate of this noise's effect on the bound when the noise level is low, specifically showing that this effect is directly proportional to the noise level and a specific constant related to dimensions.

We conducted a thorough evaluation of two Java fuzzers, EvoCrash and JCHARMING, to assess their effectiveness in replicating each other's discoveries. Our study, utilizing the same open-source codebase as the original papers, examined the extent to which these fuzzer pairs can generate the same or similar crash reports. We found that both fuzzer pairs achieved a high level of crash reproduction success, with each pair able to replicate approximately 70% of the other's crashes. Furthermore, both researchers found that nearly 90% of the unique crashes discovered by each fuzzer in individual fuzzer-vs-fuzzer runs were the result of single instructions. However, the analysis also revealed that each fuzzer discovered a significantly larger number of out-of-bounds memory access crashes compared to its counterpart in 99% of the tested scenarios.

The effects of a magnetic field on the formation of charge stripes in the high-temperature superconductor La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$ have been investigated using high-resolution NMR spectroscopy. The study focused on the changes in vortex lattice arrangement, which was observed to transition to charge stripe states at a specific temperature-dependent magnetic field, resulting in the formation of vortex lattice clusters at even higher temperatures. This process was studied in detail at a specific hole doping level, which revealed that the stripes exhibit periodicity, which varied with low temperatures, as exhibited by the appearance of distinct NMR lines. Moreover, the study revealed that a magnetic field caused a significant anisotropic shift in the Cu-NMR chemical shift, indicating that stripes form along the length of the crystal's b-axis, which agrees with prior x-ray findings.

This research aims to determine if thermal photons can provide a reliable method to examine the impact of viscous corrections on fluid behavior through comparison with other fluids. We performed a detailed investigation of anisotropic flow patterns in various models, including viscous fluids and transport equations, to understand their behavior in different scenarios. Our results reveal that while viscous corrections suppress the anisotropic flow patterns of other fluids, they surprisingly enhance the patterns of thermal photons, indicating that these patterns are influenced by different factors. We discovered that the enhanced patterns are linked to the fluid's expansion characteristics rather than its initial state. Furthermore, our analysis shows that the differences between the various models diminish with time, suggesting that the initial variations in behavior may not persist long-term.

Our research focuses on identifying and analyzing spin models with non-adjacent magnetic interactions that exhibit regular magnetic ordering in the presence of non-$O(3)$ spin rotations. We discover that such models can be visualized as closed shapes formed by a set of planar polygons, with vertices that represent lattice sites. We further establish that the regular magnetic ordering in these models is linked to specific types of chiral modes, which correspond to regular polygons inscribed within the spanning shape's chiral faces. We identify and analyze a particular category of models featuring non-adjacent interactions that support multiple regular magnetic ordering types. Notably, we introduce a novel model called the planar cube where spins interact across specific non-adjacent sites, exhibiting six distinct regular magnetic ordering types. Additionally, our research involves examining the characteristics of excited spin waves in specific models with interactions between nearest and next-nearest lattice sites, ultimately allowing us to visualize the spin wave patterns in terms of the regular magnetic ordering types they may obscure.

In the context of A/B testing, which is a common approach for evaluating the impact of changes, companies often struggle to balance detection sensitivity and the ethical implications of blind experimentation. This is particularly true when the goal is to maximize the ability to detect significant effects while minimizing potential risks associated with users experiencing no change. This challenge is especially pronounced when sample sizes are limited, resulting in small average treatment effects and low statistical power. To address this issue, a new adaptive testing framework, called AdaB, has been developed. This innovative approach allows for real-time adaptation of arm assignments, which in turn maximizes the ability to detect significant effects. Through theoretical and empirical evaluations, AdaB has been shown to significantly outperform traditional methods, including standard and ethical blind testing strategies. This is supported by applications in real-world scenarios, including an analysis of Twitter's features and a simulation of Facebook's design changes, where AdaB demonstrates improved detection rates and reduced exposure to unchangeable conditions.

The foundational aspects of cosmological inflation, a model of the universe's rapid early expansion, are explored in this paper. The discussion delves into the underlying theory of inflation, examining the universe's dynamics during the inflationary epoch through the lens of the Hamilton-Jacobi formalism. Key parameters of the slow-roll inflationary model are introduced and the condition for the end of inflation is analyzed. The paper presents an example of how to apply the Hamilton-Jacobi formalism to a specific single-field inflationary model. Furthermore, the connection between the Hamilton-Jacobi theory and the observable properties of the cosmic microwave background and large-scale structure is briefly discussed.

The CDF II collaboration recently published a precise measurement of the W boson mass. 
In a scenario where the weak interaction sector is described by the Two Higgs Doublet Model, 
a calculation of the radiative correction to the W boson mass is carried out, taking into account the effects of loop particles. 
A comparison is made between the CDF II measurement and the predicted W boson mass, assuming that the Standard Model is correct. 
This results in a discrepancy of 3.3 sigma. 
Furthermore, an examination of the possible difference between the two $W$ boson mass measurements obtained by CDF II and ATLAS collaboration is performed. 
A calculation of the predicted discrepancy is carried out, assuming that the Two Higgs Doublet Model is the correct description of the physical world. 
In this scenario, the observed discrepancy between the two W boson mass measurements can be attributed to the mass splitting between the two Higgs doublet components and would result in a corresponding difference of two times the electric charge of an electron.

Software developers who perform maintenance tasks on existing systems face
significant challenges in understanding and interpreting change requests,
where developers typically rely on existing knowledge of source code and domain
expertise. However, open-source projects may lack clear documentation, making
it difficult for contributors to dedode context relevant information. As
search efficiency is critical to minimizing change requests, this study aims to
improve the effectiveness of search results by optimizing the terms used in
change requests. To this end, it proposes a novel approach to automatically
generate and evaluate search terms from change requests by utilizing
automated testing methodologies. This, in turn, enables a precise measurement of
search term quality based on the successful execution of code modifications.

Human-to-human communication is characterized by dynamic interactions, 
whereby individuals' actions and reactions are continuously influenced and modified 
by one another's utterances. In dialogue systems, achieving this dynamic interaction 
is complicated by the fact that current generation techniques often overlook the 
interaction of this kind. In this study, a new model for text-based dialogue has been 
developed that explores and captures the concept of entrainment - the phenomenon in 
which a speaker adapts their speech to mirror their conversation partner's vocal 
characteristics. By utilizing a spoken word transcription input to simulate and model 
entrament, our dialogue system effectively produces natural-sounding responses in 
dialogue. Evaluation experiments confirm that our text generation approach 
successfully replicates entrainment and significantly enhances the quality of 
dialogue system responses.

We've developed an open-source suite of open-data simulations, designed to simplify the process of inferring properties of galaxies, stars, and other celestial objects from their spectral energy distributions. This can be achieved through photometry in multiple bands, spectra, or a combination of both. This work builds upon the work of Aakretion (Vazquez-Medina et al. 2019), with the goal of simplifying the process of fitting SFDs to a broad range of celestial objects. This project utilizes synthetic data and advanced algorithms to fit SFDs, with the goal of making it more robust and efficient. This project is compatible with popular tools such as PyEmission, and with various data formats including SED-Fits, making it easier for the scientific community to access and use the simulations. This project aims to provide a reliable framework for the process of SFD fitting, with the potential to be applied to a wide range of celestial objects and phenomena.

Classifying every video frame into its respective action is a complex task, but it's crucial for understanding the overall video. Traditional methods require a database of labeled videos, which is not only time-consuming to annotate but also limits the methods' applicability. To overcome these drawbacks, we've developed SSCAP, a novel, unsupervised approach that can identify actions in videos without prior labeling. SSCAP uses a self-supervised method to learn from a large set of videos and a novel loss function that considers temporal relationships within the videos. As a result, SSCAP can accurately segment video actions using only a single, pre-trained model. To further improve SSCAP's performance on new, unrelated videos, we've created a transfer-learning approach that allows the method to adapt to different domains. SSCAP's performance was successfully demonstrated through its application to human motion and animal behavior datasets.

We explore the existence of seven hadronic molecular states consisting of $\bar D^{(*)} \Sigma_c^{(*)}$, which may form bound or virtual states due to the one-loop one-pion exchange mechanism. By combining this with a contact interaction, we use a relativistic three-body equation to investigate the properties of these states. Utilizing the dressed quark model, we calculate one-pion exchange forces and contact terms, then determine bounds on coupling constants to establish bounds on contact interactions. Our simulations reveal that only $\bar D \Sigma_c^{*}$ and $\bar D^{*} \Sigma_c^{*}$ can potentially form molecular states. Furthermore, in the weak decay process $D^{*+} \Sigma_c^- \to e^+ \nu_e p$, we explore the effects of final-state interactions among $\bar D^{(*)} \Sigma_c^-$ and $p$.

The education community has expressed concern over the lack of testing knowledge and skills among graduates, prompting calls for action. Researchers have introduced innovative teaching methods to address this gap, yet the teaching of testing itself poses significant challenges due to testing's limited scope and diverse applications. To address these challenges, this study employs an outcome-based education approach, focusing on teaching core concepts and skills rather than specific tools or techniques. We employed two teaching methods, one inquiry-based and the other lecture-based, to examine their effectiveness in teaching these principles. Our results indicate that the inquiry-based method led to better learning outcomes, deeper understanding of testing activities, and improved test design skills, while also allowing for more efficient use of class time.

Domain adaptation is a machine learning approach that adapts models to target domains using data from source domains. It is particularly effective when the target domain has limited or no labels. Our proposed method, Domain Adaptation via Cross Loss Minimization, leverages semi-supervised learning to enhance results by cross-training models and utilizing label information. This is achieved by minimizing three loss functions: classification loss, reconstruction loss, and cross regularization loss. This technique has achieved state-of-the-art results in various domain adaptation tasks, including image, speech, and text domains, and has significantly improved existing methods.

A unique reactor design, the Gas Core Reactor (GCR), is introduced in this study and analyzed. A crucial component of this reactor, the fuel source, is being developed at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. This paper delves into the fundamentals of this reactor concept, including its internal workings and overall layout. A comprehensive thermal-mechanical analysis of the GCR's core is presented, focusing on the interactions between the fuel source and the surrounding coolant. Additionally, the analysis covers the examination of core internals, structural analysis of supporting components, and the evaluation of neutron shielding in gasket materials used in the core. Furthermore, the study explores the potential issues of fuel droplet evaporation and burning within the core, including the analysis of local burning patterns and overall burnup. A detailed analysis of the GCR's overall performance, including the examination of core and outer vessel temperatures, is presented as well. This study aims to provide insight into the potential application of the GCR in generating electricity through the generation of high-velocity jets of fuel droplets.

This study introduces a novel neural network architecture designed to predict particle interactions localized to specific detector regions efficiently. By integrating neural network capabilities with a Gaussian process model, our method addresses the challenge of handling complex particle collisions in high-energy experiments without incurring the computational cost of a global model. We develop a Domain-informed Neural Network that combines these elements, combining a small multilayer perceptron domain input with a Gaussian process model that incorporates domain-specific prior information. In comparison to traditional multilayer perceptrons trained locally, DiNN demonstrates significant improvements, achieving reduced mean squared error of predicted particle energies by a factor of 1.72 and reduced prediction time with an improvement of an order of magnitude. Furthermore, we demonstrate a strong correlation between DiNN's prior knowledge and actual detection areas within the detector, allowing for flexible control over inference speed and accuracy.

The spectral analysis of substellar objects relies heavily on accurate data regarding their molecular absorption capabilities. However, this data is often based on older models that may not be entirely reliable. This study compares the spectral signatures of T dwarfs observed in actual data and synthetic models with those generated using various molecular cross-sections for H2O, CH4, and CO. It's found that the water molecule's absorption spectrum has a significant impact on the observed $y$-band brightness, while changes in the absorption of methane and carbon monoxide greatly affect the observed $J$-band brightness. These comparisons highlight discrepancies between old and new cross-section models that could lead to inaccuracies in determining the temperature profiles and atmospheric properties of T dwarfs.

This text offers an in-depth explanation of a formal method for a grounding algorithm of Answer Set Programming with the ground(Ast) predicate, which is used to determine which terms can be used in a program. The explanation uses well-established theories and well-defined operators to underpin the development of a clear and intuitive structure for the description, which is based on the work of Allez et al. (2019). The description draws on the theories of first-order logic and ground formulas, as well as the theories of order and weakly ordered sets, to develop a clear structure for describing the algorithm. The result is a clear axiomatic framework that can be used to implement a grounding algorithm for Answer Set Programming in general modules.

We have extended resource theory methods to handle complex multi-resource scenarios, focusing on situations where multiple types of resources are converted into one usable form. By using relative entropy measurements, we can determine the lower bound of required resources and establish upper and lower bounds on their actual requirements. In a specific case of DNA and energy resources, our approach determines the optimal ways cells utilize energy to replicate DNA accurately.

This study investigates a certain type of estimation problem in which one seeks to approximate a random vector's projection onto a specific subspace, which is defined by noisy measurements. The performance measure used to assess the quality of this approximation is the mean-square error between the estimate and the actual random vector projection. It's demonstrated that an upper bound can be placed on this performance measure, which is determined by conditions that are equivalent to those found in a well-known bound related to the Kullback-Leibler divergence. This new bound is specifically applicable to a diverse set of scenarios such as complex AWGN channels, real AWGN channels, and Rayleigh fading with complex AWGN channels. Moreover, in the Gaussian channel scenario, a certain type of estimate is proven to achieve optimal performance.

This research investigates the joint behavior of certain unit root test statistics when the data exhibits multiple stochastic trends, focusing on both local and local-to-random nonstationities. By assuming that trends are linear with random coefficients and include exogenous variables, we develop new asymptotic distributions for these test statistics using functional rank-correlation methods. These findings are relevant for determining the number of stochastic trends in a time series and can be applied to a broader class of estimators and test statistics that rely on eigenvalues of a specific matrix product.

A novel quantum error correction code, termed the polar code, has been developed with the aim of achieving near-optimal performance in correcting errors while maintaining a linear relationship between codeword length and error correction capabilities. This innovative code was recently proposed in [1] and demonstrates successful correction of errors under a specific type of error model, with a corresponding rate that scales linearly with its error correcting capacity. 

We have successfully adapted the construction method initially designed for classical low-density parity check codes to create polar LDPC quantum codes. By applying a recursive process to both the eigenvalues of the symplectic matrix and a parameter $m$, we can determine a quantum code with parameters depending on these values. 

Through a detailed analysis, it has been shown that polar LDPC quantum codes outperform random quantum LDPC codes when experiencing simultaneous errors, and we have established a range within which their error correcting threshold surpasses those achieved previously. 

Furthermore, employing a variant of the belief propagation algorithm, we have designed a decoder for these codes that demonstrates convergence when the given codeword is error-free, and conversely, shows failure to converge when the codeword contains an error, assuming specific noise thresholds are met.

The problem of finding a $r$-distance dominating set of a graph, known to be NP-hard, becomes even more challenging when dealing with larger distances. A $p$-approximation algorithm is developed for this problem, with parameters influenced by the radius of graphs of distance at most $r$. The efficiency of this algorithm, $p$-approximate D$^r$S, depends on the graph's distance at most $r$ and reaches its worst case in scenarios where $r$ equals $n-1$. A key benefit of this algorithm, D$^r$S, is its capacity to solve the $r$-distance dominating set problem for graphs exhibiting a small $r$-domination number, $γ_r(G)$. Furthermore, a lower bound of $2^{r/27} - 1$ is established for the approximation ratio of the D$^r$S problem, supported by an additional lower bound of $2^{r/27} - 1$ for the $r$-domination problem itself.

This research examines the robustness of two-dimensional topological insulators of the 4th order in a continuous system under various forms of disorder. We investigate how disorder impacts the protected states at the system's edges by analyzing the participation ratios of the wave functions. We discover that certain topological insulator configurations maintain their resistance when subjected to non-correlated disorder, whereas others collapse when exposed to correlated disorder affecting the system's Hamiltonian.

This article presents initial findings from a search for highly massive gluinos in a supersymmetric model where supersymmetry is not preserved by soft terms. Heavy gluinos are produced in pairs and decay into a final state containing bottom quarks and significant energy from hadronic collisions. Initial results from a 37.3 TeV proton-proton collision in 2021 show a data set that is consistent with standard model predictions, establishing maximum signal limits for various scenarios. In one specific scenario where the mass difference between the gluino and bottom quark is 1000 GeV, the 95% confidence level upper bounds on the production cross-section are 0.036 pb, and the corresponding upper bounds on the production cross-section for heavier gluino pairs are 0.0001 pb. This corresponds to exclusion limits for masses up to 1800 GeV.

Novel view synthesis from unoccupied viewpoints is a key capability in computer graphics, yet achieving photorealistic results remains challenging due to factors like complex lighting and material properties. We introduce a model that learns to generate novel views of scenes based on arbitrary point queries using a database of real-world images. Our approach stands out among real-world scene representation models due to its ability to use a four-dimensional light field model, leading to more efficient processing and improved handling of intricate shading effects. Furthermore, this representation in combination with an image generation model and an optimization process significantly enhances the ability to synthesize novel views and improves overall accuracy compared to existing methods.

Observations of the close binary system BD$+66^{\circ}$$+$\,$$223$ were conducted at the LCO observatory in 2020 and LCO's astrophysics team performed orbit monitoring. The goal was to detect orbital motion and track changes in magnitude. The observation objectives included detecting changes in magnitude and orbital motion, as well as searching for the presence of additional close companions or transiting objects. The observation results showed no changes in magnitude and no additional close companions or transiting objects were found. The primary objective of observing close binary systems is to detect changes in magnitude and/or orbital motion over time. The observation results of this study show no changes in magnitude and no additional close companions or transiting objects were found. The observation objectives of this study were to detect changes in magnitude and/or orbital motion over time and to search for the presence of additional close companions or transiting objects. The observation results of this study show no changes in magnitude and no additional close companions or transiting objects were found.
